recipes.name: Baingan Bharta (smoky roasted eggplant mash) with whole-wheat roti
recipes.seasonWhy: Brinjal/eggplant is a rainy-season crop in India — planted Jun–Jul, harvested through late monsoon Sep/Oct; abundant in markets Aug–Sep. Tomatoes, onions, green chilies, fresh coriander also monsoon-season staples.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Naturally soft-mashed — just skip the green chilies, use a little less Kashmiri chili powder, and mash it extra smooth. The roasted-garlic sweetness comes through for little ones, and the scoop-and-dip format with roti is one kids love.

groups.title: Roasting (before any pot)
items: 1 large brinjal/baingan (eggplant), ~450–500 g — choose one with shiny smooth skin, relatively light for its size (fewer seeds, less bitterness)
1 tsp oil, for greasing the skin (chars evenly, peels easier)
3 garlic cloves, peeled + 1 green chili (to stuff into the slits)

groups.title: Tadka / tempering (oil first, then seeds)
items: 2½ tbsp mustard oil (or neutral oil for a milder flavor) — heat till it just smokes, then cool a minute to tame the pungency
1 dried red chili, broken in half

groups.title: Aromatics (into the crackling oil)
items: 1–2 green chilies, slit lengthwise (use 1 or skip for a milder bharta)

groups.title: Tomato + spice base
items: 1 tsp salt (draws juices out of the tomatoes so they break down faster)
½ tsp Kashmiri red chili powder

groups.title: Main body (last big addition)
items: Roasted eggplant pulp from Stage 0 (~350 g mashed flesh)

groups.title: Finishing (off/after heat)
items: 1 tsp kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves) — crush between palms
2 tbsp fresh coriander leaves (cilantro), chopped, plus more to garnish

method: Rinse, dry, and grease the brinjal with the 1 tsp oil. Make 4 deep slits around it and tuck the garlic cloves and green chili inside. Place directly over a gas flame (or under a very hot grill/broiler) and roast 10–12 min, turning every 2–3 min with tongs, until the skin is blackened all over and the flesh collapses when pressed. (Oven/air-fryer works but loses the signature smoky flavor.)

Rest 10 min — covering the hot brinjal steams the skin loose. Peel off the charred skin (leave a few charred flecks for smokiness). Scoop the pulp into a bowl and mash with a fork; chop the roasted garlic and chili in with it.
Heat the mustard oil in a heavy kadai/pan over medium-high until it just begins to smoke lightly; take off the heat for a minute to cool slightly, then return to medium.
Add the cumin seeds and dried red chili. When the cumin crackles and darkens (~20 sec), add the chopped ginger and garlic; sauté ~1 min until the raw smell disappears.
Add the onion and slit green chilies; sauté 3–4 min until the onion softens and turns golden at the edges.

Add the tomatoes and salt; cook 4–5 min until the tomatoes turn soft and mushy and oil begins to glisten at the edges. Add the turmeric, coriander powder, Kashmiri chili, and cumin powder; fry 1 min until the masala darkens and smells aromatic.
Add the mashed eggplant; mix and mash together 4–5 min, until one smoky, glossy, well-combined mash. Adjust salt.
Off the heat: stir in the garam masala, crushed kasuri methi, coriander leaves, and lemon juice. Rest 2 min, garnish, and serve hot with whole-wheat roti.
recipes.story: Baingan bharta was born in Punjab's villages, where farmers buried whole eggplants in the dying embers of the clay tandoor after the day's bread was baked — the slow char giving the flesh its signature smokiness. The roasted pulp was mashed ("bharta" literally means "mashed") with mustard oil, onion, and village-ground spices for a hearty farmer's meal. It's still the dish Punjabis make when they want the taste of an open fire at the lunch table.

sources.name: Tarla Dalal — Smoky Baingan Bharta Recipe (Punjabi Style)

recipes.name: Bruschetta al Pomodoro
recipes.seasonWhy: September in Tuscany — vine-ripe tomatoes in their final flush (good April through end of September), fresh basil still harvestable before fall frosts, garlic year-round, olive oil pantry-available year-round.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Mild, finger-friendly, and eaten with hands the authentic way — just keep the garlic rub light. Make mini bruschette on small toast rounds for little hands.

groups.title: Bread prep
items: 12 slices rustic Tuscan-style bread (pane toscano — plain Tuscan bread made from just flour, water, and yeast; classically unsalted, "pane sciocco" — egg-free and dairy-free), about ½-inch thick (from roughly a 500 g loaf)
1 large garlic clove, halved crosswise (for rubbing the toast)
2 tbsp extra virgin olive oil, for the bread

groups.title: Tomato topping
items: 900 g (about 2 lb / 6 medium) ripe vine-ripe or Roma tomatoes — firm but fully ripe, cored, cut into ¼-inch dice
8–10 large fresh basil leaves, torn by hand or cut chiffonade
1 small garlic clove, peeled and lightly smashed (marinates with the tomatoes, removed before serving)

groups.title: Finish
items: Extra virgin olive oil, for drizzling

method: Toss diced tomatoes in a bowl with 3 tbsp olive oil, fine salt, torn basil, and the smashed garlic clove. Rest at room temperature 20–30 min (up to 4 hours) so the juices gather.
Toast bread slices on a grill, griddle pan, or under a hot broiler, 1–3 min per side, until golden — crisp outside, still soft inside.
While each slice is still hot, rub one side gently with the cut face of the halved garlic clove (light pressure — flavor, not chunks).
Drizzle toasted slices with 2 tbsp olive oil.
Fish the smashed garlic clove out of the tomato mix. Spoon marinated tomatoes generously over each slice.
Finish with flaky sea salt and a final thread of olive oil. Serve immediately, on a board or plate, not stacked.
recipes.story: Bruschetta takes its name from the Italian verb bruscare — "to roast or toast," referring to bread roasted over coals. It began in Ancient Rome as simple toasted bread with local olive oil; tomatoes only joined the topping after the 15th century, when they arrived from the Americas. In Tuscany it has its own name, fettunta ("oily slice"), and the custom of rubbing grilled bread with raw garlic grew out of farmers tasting each autumn's first pressing of new olive oil on hot bread.

recipes.name: Kuri Gohan
recipes.seasonWhy: Fresh Japanese chestnuts (kuri) harvest Sep–Nov — mid-September is when the first fresh crop appears in Kansai markets; the Tamba region in northern Kansai is one of Japan's most famous chestnut-growing areas. New-harvest rice (shinmai) arrives in autumn too (late Sep/Oct) — seasonally ideal pairing.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Already a beloved kids' dish in Japan — sweet, mild, and soft. Omit the sake (flavor unchanged — salt and kombu carry it), halve large chestnuts, and skip the sesame for little ones. It packs well as chestnut rice balls (onigiri) for lunchboxes.

groups.title: Rice prep
items: 2 cups (400 g) Japanese short-grain white rice
⅓ cup (60 g) sweet/glutinous rice (mochigome — sticky Japanese rice; or substitute extra short-grain rice)
Water for rinsing + 2¼ cups (540 ml) for cooking

groups.title: Chestnuts
items: 20–25 fresh chestnuts (~400 g; halve large ones after peeling)

groups.title: Seasoning (added with rice, before cooking)
items: One 5 cm (2 in) square kombu (dried kelp seaweed — used for umami; removed before serving)
1 tbsp sake (Japanese rice wine), optional — omit for kid version

groups.title: Finishing
items: 1 tbsp toasted black sesame seeds, to sprinkle

method: Prep chestnuts. Soak in warm water 30 min to soften shells. With a paring knife, cut off the flat bottom, peel the hard outer shell in strips base-to-tip, then peel the thin papery brown inner skin. Drop peeled chestnuts into a bowl of water, changing water 2–3 times; soak 30 min. Shortcut: vacuum-packed pre-peeled chestnuts — skip peeling, rinse and soak 15 min.
Rinse rice. Both rices in a bowl, cover with cold water, swirl with hand, pour off cloudy water; repeat 3–4 times until nearly clear. Drain well (or rest in strainer 15 min).

Load the pot. Drained rice + 2¼ cups water in a heavy pot or rice cooker. Add salt, sake (if using), and kombu; stir gently. Lay chestnuts on top in a single layer. Rest 20–30 min so rice absorbs water evenly.
Cook. Bring to boil over medium heat, reduce to low, cover, cook 12–13 min until water is absorbed. (Rice cooker: regular setting.)
Steam. Remove from heat, rest with lid on 15–20 min. Do not skip — this finishes the chestnuts.
Serve. Discard kombu. Fluff gently with a rice paddle, folding chestnuts in; sprinkle with black sesame seeds.
recipes.story: Kuri gohan is one of Japan's quintessential autumn rice dishes — when the first chestnuts (kuri) appear in markets from September, families steam them with new-harvest rice to celebrate the season. In Kansai, home of the famed Tamba chestnuts, it's a classic autumn table dish, often served during the moon-viewing (tsukimi) season when autumn's harvest is at its fullest.

sources.name: MAFF Japan "Our Regional Cuisines" via Fukuchiyama City Rural Women's Council

recipes.name: Empanadas de Espinaca y Queso
recipes.seasonWhy: September = early spring in the Southern Hemisphere; Mendoza's cool spring markets carry fresh cool-season greens — spinach (espinaca) and acelga (Swiss chard, the classic Argentine leafy green) are both at home in an early-spring filling.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Naturally kid-friendly: hand-held, no knife needed, mild. Chop the spinach very fine (no visible green bits for picky eaters) and go light on the nutmeg; optionally make 18 mini empanadas for smaller portions.

groups.title: Dough (masa criolla, egg-free)
items: (No egg — verified egg-free across all dough sources)

groups.title: Filling: greens
items: 500 g fresh spinach, washed — or acelga (Swiss chard; stems removed, leaves used)

groups.title: Cheeses + seasoning
items: 250 g mozzarella or queso cremoso, cut into 12 cubes
Salt and black pepper, to taste

method: Make the dough. Mix flour and salt in a large bowl. Make a well, add the oil, then pour in warm water gradually while working the flour in. Knead 8–10 min until smooth, soft, and elastic. Cover and rest 30 min at room temperature.
Blanch the greens. Plunge spinach (or acelga leaves) into boiling salted water 1 min, drain, rinse under cold water, squeeze out ALL the water with your hands, chop finely.
Sauté the base. Melt butter in a saucepan over medium heat; sauté onion 5–6 min until soft and translucent; add garlic, cook 1 min.

Build the salsa blanca. Stir cornstarch into the onion mixture until coated (paste). Pour in the milk all at once and whisk constantly over medium-low heat until thick enough to hold its shape, 3–4 min.
Finish the filling. Stir in the grated hard cheese, fold in the chopped greens. Season with salt, pepper, nutmeg. Cool completely.
Roll the discs. Divide dough into 12 balls; roll each ~14 cm wide, ~3 mm thick — not paper-thin, or the juicy filling bursts through.

Assemble. ~2 tbsp filling per disc, one mozzarella/queso cremoso cube on top, moisten edge with water, fold, press, and finish with a repulgue (the classic Argentine rope-twist crimp) or press with a fork.
Bake. 200°C (390°F), 18–22 min, until deep golden. Rest 5 min — the cheese center is molten.
recipes.story: Empanadas came to Argentina with Spanish colonizers, who brought the medieval Iberian tradition of savory filled pastries to the Río de la Plata centuries ago. Each Argentine province then made the empanada its own: Mendoza — in the Cuyo region at the foot of the Andes — claims la mendocina, traditionally a beef-and-onion empanada judged at empanada festivals as a symbol of provincial identity. The signature crimped edge, the repulgue, is itself a craft: a rope-twist seal that locks in the filling and, in street stalls, signals what's inside. Spinach-and-cheese fillings grew out of Argentina's broader tradition — early Italian immigration made greens and soft cheese a staple filling — and today they're among the most popular vegetarian empanadas nationwide, sold in Mendoza's street stalls alongside the classic beef ones.

sources.name: Cookpad Argentina — Norali, Empanadas de espinaca, salsa blanca y queso

recipes.name: Gudeg
recipes.seasonWhy: Java's dry season runs Apr–Oct, so September is the dry-season tail. Young jackfruit (nangka muda) fruits year-round, but the long-braised pot favors dry-season staples — coconut, palm sugar, long-storing produce — making this slow-simmered comfort dish a natural dry-season dinner.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Natural — sweet, mild, and soft-simmered for hours until the jackfruit goes spoon-tender. No adaptation needed; just keep the sambal away from their portion.

groups.title: Pre-boil
items: 1 kg young jackfruit (nangka muda — young green jackfruit; unripe, firm, starchy flesh), peeled, seeded, cut into 2-inch pieces — or 2 cans (800 g) green jackfruit in brine, drained and rinsed

groups.title: Bumbu halus (ground spice paste)
items: 4 candlenuts (kemiri — rich, oily nut used as a thickener; substitute raw macadamia if unavailable), toasted 2 min
(Blend everything to a smooth paste with 2–3 tbsp water.)

groups.title: Braise
items: 150–200 g palm sugar (gula aren/gula jawa), shaved
1½ tsp salt, plus more to taste
2 black tea bags (color substitute for daun jati teak leaves — tea gives the color; teak leaves give the tradition)

groups.title: To serve
items: Optional sambal on the side (adults only for kids' portions)

method: Boil the jackfruit pieces in plenty of water 20–30 min to soften and remove the raw edge. Drain. (Canned: rinse well, boil 10 min.) Lightly bruise pieces with a pestle or knife handle — helps the spices penetrate.
Blend the bumbu halus components to a smooth paste with 2–3 tbsp water.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Sauté the paste 5–7 min until deep golden and fragrant, oil glistening at the edges.
Add jackfruit, daun salam, galangal, and lemongrass; toss 3 min to coat.
Pour in the thin coconut milk plus enough water to just submerge everything. Add palm sugar, salt, and tea bags. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce to the lowest simmer.
Simmer 3–4 hr, partially covered, stirring every 30 min. The liquid reduces; the jackfruit turns reddish-brown and silky.

Remove tea bags and leaves. Pour in the thick coconut milk; simmer 30–45 min more until the sauce is nearly dry and everything is coated in a glossy, dark braise. Taste: sweet first, gently savory after, salt to finish.
Rest 15 min. Serve warm over steamed rice with fried shallots and sambal on the side.
recipes.story: Gudeg was born in the 16th century during the founding of the Islamic Mataram kingdom at Alas Mentaok, the forest clearing that became Kotagede — the seed of modern Yogyakarta. As the forest was cut down to build the new court, workers were surrounded by felled young jackfruit trees — fruit considered too ordinary to sell — plus coconut palms at the forest's edge. They cooked the young jackfruit, called gori, in huge cauldrons with coconut milk and spices, stirring for hours with long wooden spoons so a meal could feed hundreds. In Javanese that constant stirring is called hangudeg — and the name stuck. Over centuries it rose from workers' food to the court's table, and the Javanese read meaning into it: the long, patient cooking stands for perseverance (alon-alon asal kelakon — slowly but surely it gets done), and the dominant sweetness for the gentleness and hospitality of Yogyakarta's people. The signature deep brown color comes from teak leaves simmered in the pot — no soy sauce, no caramel.

recipes.name: Quesadillas de Huitlacoche
recipes.seasonWhy: Huitlacoche (Mexican corn truffle) grows on corn ears during the rainy season and is harvested fresh roughly June–October — September is peak season, when it fills Oaxacan market stalls and street comals.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Naturally kid-friendly: hand-held, mild, cheesy. Keep the serrano/jalapeño out entirely for kids; chop the huitlacoche fine (the dark color is the "spooky-cool" selling point — call it the Mexican truffle). Halve the epazote in their portion; queso Oaxaca + corn tortilla is universally kid-approved.

groups.title: The filling base (sauté first)
items: 1 poblano chile, roasted, peeled, and cut into thin strips
½ jalapeño or serrano chile, seeded and finely chopped (optional; keep it mild for kids)

groups.title: Huitlacoche (the star)
items: 500 g fresh huitlacoche (Mexican corn truffle), cleaned and roughly chopped — or 2 cans (~400 g drained), liquid drained
1 tsp fine salt, plus more to taste
Splash of water (only if using canned and the pan is dry)

groups.title: Herb + cheese (added last)
items: 6–8 fresh epazote leaves, chopped — or 1 tbsp dried
300 g queso Oaxaca (Oaxacan string cheese), pulled into strings (fresh mozzarella works)

groups.title: To serve
items: Salsa verde or roja on the side

method: Make the tortilla dough. Mix masa harina and salt; pour in warm water gradually, kneading to a soft, pliable dough (like play-dough, not crumbly). Rest 10 min covered with a damp towel.
Start the filling. Heat oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Sauté onion 4–5 min until golden-soft but not browned; add garlic and poblano strips, cook 1 min until fragrant.

Add the huitlacoche. Add huitlacoche and salt. Cook 10–15 min, stirring, until most of the moisture has evaporated and the mixture goes glossy and almost black. Keep some tenderness — moist, never mushy.
Finish with epazote. Stir in the chopped epazote, cook 2 min more, taste for salt. Set aside warm.
Press the tortillas. Divide dough into 8 balls. Press each to ~14 cm rounds, ~3 mm thick.

Cook de comal (on the griddle). Heat a dry comal or cast-iron skillet over medium-high. Lay a tortilla on; after ~40 sec flip. On the second side, immediately spread a handful of queso Oaxaca on one half, spoon over the huitlacoche filling, and fold the tortilla closed. Cook 1–2 min per side, pressing gently, until the cheese melts and the tortilla is blistered and golden in spots.
Serve. Hot, with salsa, lime, and pickled onion alongside.
recipes.story: Huitlacoche is a fungus that swells grey-blue ears of corn during the rainy season. Where most of the world saw a blight and burned it, Mexico saw a delicacy: the Aztecs were eating it centuries ago, and today it sells for more than the corn it grows on — the "Mexican truffle." In Oaxaca, it rides the rainy-season wave onto the comals: market vendors and street quesadilla-makers stir it with epazote and poblano, fold it into fresh corn tortillas with a tangle of queso Oaxaca, and hand it over blistering hot. There's a quiet poetry to it — the rains that feed the milpa also feed the fungus, and the same epazote that seasons beans seasons huitlacoche. Nothing wasted, everything in season.

recipes.name: Ratatouille Niçoise
recipes.seasonWhy: September = autumn harvest in Provence; tomatoes, eggplant, zucchini, and peppers all peak at once — ratatouille is the dish Provençal households make when the garden overflows with "légumes du soleil" (vegetables of the sun).

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Natural — soft, mild, sweet, colorful, with no heat anywhere in the dish. For picky eaters: peel the peppers (skins can be tough) or chop everything smaller; kids love it over rice or with bread for dipping.

groups.title: Vegetables (cut and prepped, salted first)
items: 1 medium eggplant (~350 g), cut into 2 cm cubes — salt the cubes, rest 15 min, rinse, pat very dry
2 medium zucchini (~400 g), cut into 2 cm cubes
1 red bell pepper + 1 yellow bell pepper, cut into 2 cm pieces
500 g ripe tomatoes, peeled, seeded, and diced (or halved cherry tomatoes)

groups.title: Fat + aromatics (go into the pot)
items: 6–8 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, added in stages
1 bouquet garni: 2–3 sprigs fresh thyme + 1 sprig rosemary + 2 bay leaves, tied together — or 2 tsp dried herbes de Provence
1½ tsp fine salt, plus more to taste

groups.title: To serve
items: Thick slices of rustic sourdough bread
Optional: crumbled goat cheese or grated Parmesan-style hard cheese

method: Salt the eggplant. Toss the cubes with 1 tsp salt, rest 15 min, rinse, and pat very dry — the key to golden (not soggy) eggplant.

Sauté each vegetable separately in a large heavy pot with 1–2 tbsp olive oil each: eggplant 5 min until golden → lift out; zucchini 4 min until lightly colored → lift out; peppers 6 min until softened → lift out.
Build the base. Add the onion with a little more oil; cook 6–8 min until soft and sweet. Add garlic, cook 1 min. Add the tomatoes and cook 5 min until they break into a sauce.

Combine and simmer. Return all vegetables to the pot. Tuck in the bouquet garni (or herbes de Provence), season with salt and pepper. Cover, lower the heat, and simmer gently 30 min, stirring occasionally — the vegetables should be tender and glazed, not falling apart.
Finish. Fish out the bouquet garni. Fold in the torn basil. Rest 10 min — ratatouille is better after a short rest, and it's genuinely wonderful at room temperature the next day.
recipes.story: Ratatouille comes from the Niçois word ratatouiller — to stir and toss together — and it was born as pure harvest logic: in late summer and early autumn, Provençal gardens produce everything at once, and this was the pot that caught it all. The rustic wisdom is in the method, not the ingredients — each vegetable sautéed separately so the eggplant doesn't mush into the zucchini, then married slowly under a bundle of thyme and bay. It's peasant food that never apologized: eaten warm, at room temperature, or the next day when the flavors have deepened, always with bread. Autumn in Provence smells like this pot.

sources.name: Asahi Press French-language textbook (Unité 8, La Provence)

recipes.name: Locro de Zapallo
recipes.seasonWhy: September in the high Andes is the dry tail before the spring rains — the highland pantry runs on stored harvests, and this is the dish that turns them into a meal. Potato and choclo harvests peak Jan–Jun, quinoa Apr–Jul, starchy maize May–Jul — all stored and sold in highland markets year-round.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Naturally kid-friendly: soft, cheesy, sweet from the squash. Keep the ají amarillo at 1 tbsp (mild and fruity, not fiery); chop the huacatay fine and use half in their bowl. Kids love the queso fresco cubes melting into the rice.

groups.title: Sofrito base (fry first)
items: 1–2 tbsp ají amarillo paste (Peruvian yellow hot pepper paste; 1 tbsp = mild, 2 = warming)
1 tsp fine salt, plus more to taste

groups.title: The stew (go in together)
items: 900 g zapallo (Andean pumpkin) — kabocha or butternut, peeled, seeded, cut in ~2.5 cm cubes
2 medium floury potatoes (~400 g), peeled, cut in ~2.5 cm cubes
1½ cups choclo (large-kernel Andean corn) kernels (frozen, thawed) — or 1 cob cut into 2 cm discs

groups.title: Beans (added near the end)
items: ½ cup green peas (fresh or frozen)
½ cup habas (broad beans), shelled (frozen, thawed; fresh if in season)

groups.title: Dairy + herb (off the heat)
items: 1 cup queso fresco (fresh white cheese), cut in cubes
2 tbsp fresh huacatay (black mint) leaves, chopped — or 2 tbsp mint + cilantro mixed

groups.title: To serve
items: Salsa criolla (Peruvian onion-lime relish) on the side, if liked

method: Build the sofrito. Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook 4–5 min until very soft but not browned. Add the garlic and ají amarillo paste; cook 3–4 min more, stirring — the paste should fry in the oil, not scorch.

Add the harvest. Add the zapallo, potatoes, choclo, salt, and water/stock. Bring to a gentle boil, lower the heat, and cook partially covered 25–30 min, until the squash starts to soften and the liquid thickens. Fold, don't stir — keep some cubes intact (locro is a thick stew, not a soup).
Add the beans. Add the peas and habas; cook 5 min more until tender. If the pot dries out, splash in more water — if too thin, cook uncovered a few minutes to reduce.

Finish off the heat. Turn off the heat. Pour in the evaporated milk, add the queso fresco cubes, and fold through — the cheese warms but stays in cubes. Scatter the huacatay, season with pepper and more salt, and serve immediately over rice.
recipes.story: "Locro" comes from the Quechua ruqru — stew — and this pot is older than the Inca Empire: the high Andes learned long ago how to keep harvests alive through the dry months (freeze-dried chuño potatoes, stored grains, dried beans), and locro is the dish that turns the stored harvest into comfort. Zapallo, papa, choclo, habas — the four pillars of the highland pantry — melted down with ají amarillo and finished with huacatay, the herb that makes a Peruvian nose recognize home. On the September table, before the spring rains begin, this is what the Andes taste like: sweet squash, starchy corn, and patience.

recipes.name: Moqueca de Palmito
recipes.seasonWhy: Bahia is tropical — moqueca's ingredients (palmito, coconut, dendê, peppers, tomato, coentro) are year-round market staples, not seasonal visitors. Late September marks the end of the dry season as spring arrives: the comfort of a slow, coconut-creamy stew lands exactly right on the cusp.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Natural — mild, creamy, no heat: the peppers cook down sweet and the coconut milk softens everything. Go light on the dendê in their bowl (its flavor is intense); palmito is soft and artichoke-mild, and kids tend to love it over rice.

groups.title: Sauté base (go in first)
items: 1 tbsp dendê (red palm oil) + 1 tbsp neutral oil (or olive oil)
1 red pimentão (bell pepper) + 1 green pimentão (bell pepper), sliced into rings
1 tsp fine salt, plus more to taste

groups.title: The stew (go in together)
items: 1 can (400 g) palmito (hearts of palm), drained and sliced into 1 cm rounds
2 medium tomatoes, sliced into rings (or 1 can diced tomatoes, drained)
1 can (400 ml) leite de coco (coconut milk), well shaken

groups.title: Finish (added last, off or near-off the heat)
items: ½ cup coentro (coriander leaf/cilantro) leaves, roughly chopped
A drizzle more dendê (optional, for color)

groups.title: To serve
items: Optional pirão (cassava-flour porridge): whisk 3 tbsp fine manioc flour into 1 cup of the hot stew broth off the heat until it thickens to a soft porridge

method: Start the base. Heat the dendê and oil in a large heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion and cook 4–5 min until soft and translucent; add the garlic and cook 1 min more.
Soften the peppers. Add the pimentões, salt, and paprika; cook 4–5 min, stirring, until the peppers soften and the oil turns sunset-orange.

Layer the stew. Add the palmito rounds and tomato rings, nestling them in. Pour the leite de coco evenly over everything; add the cumin if using. Bring to the barest simmer — never a vigorous boil, which can split the coconut milk.
Simmer gently. Reduce the heat to low, partially cover, and cook 15–20 min, until the peppers and tomatoes are fully tender and the sauce has thickened slightly. Taste for salt.

Finish Bahian-style. Take off the heat. Stir in the lime juice and most of the coentro; drizzle the extra dendê if you like the color. Rest 5 min, then serve over rice with pirão alongside and the remaining coentro on top.
recipes.story: Moqueca is Bahia's soul dish — an Afro-Brazilian inheritance cooked in a clay panela de barro, built on three pillars that all came across the Atlantic from West Africa: dendê, coconut, and coentro. The classic is fish, caught that morning in the Baía de Todos os Santos; moqueca de palmito is the vegetarian answer, and a proud one — the tender palm hearts soak up the dendê-coconut broth the way fish never could. In Salvador, moqueca is Friday food, eaten slowly, with rice and pirão and lime. This is dinner as the Bahians do it: golden, fragrant, and unhurried.

recipes.name: Espinacas con Garbanzos
recipes.seasonWhy: Spinach is an autumn leafy green in southern Spain; chickpeas are the dried-pulse staple of autumn stews — this is the dish of cuaresma (Lent), when Seville's tavern cooks lean on chickpeas, greens, and the ancient bread-cumin-vinegar paste.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Skip the guindilla and use only sweet paprika — the soft chickpeas and mild spinach are toddler-friendly. Lightly mash a portion of the chickpeas for under-5s.

groups.title: Chickpeas (garbanzos)
items: 3 cups cooked chickpeas (~2 × 400 g cans, drained and rinsed), OR 180 g dried chickpeas soaked overnight and simmered 60–90 min until tender

groups.title: The majado (flavor paste — every component pounded together)
items: 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil (aceite de oliva virgen extra)
2 thick slices day-old rustic bread (pan de pueblo)
~120 ml warm water or the spinach-blanching water

groups.title: Finish
items: 1 dried guindilla (small Spanish red chili) — optional

method: If using dried chickpeas: soak overnight; next day simmer with the bay leaf until creamy-tender (60–90 min); drain. If canned: rinse well.
Blanch the spinach in well-salted boiling water for 2–3 min until just wilted; drain, rinse with cold water, squeeze out as much water as possible with your hands, and chop roughly.
Heat the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Fry the whole garlic cloves until golden (not dark), then fry the bread slices until crisp. Lift both out.

In a mortar, pound the fried garlic and bread with the cumin, paprika, and a splash of sherry vinegar; loosen with a little warm water or spinach water until you have a thick, rustic paste (the majado).
In the same pan, add the chickpeas with a ladle of warm water (and the guindilla, if using); stir in the majado and simmer 10 min so the chickpeas drink up the flavor.
Fold in the chopped spinach; simmer 5 min more until the stew is thick and glossy. Taste and salt.
Rest 10 min off the heat. Serve warm in bowls with a drizzle of olive oil and crusty bread for mopping.
recipes.story: In Seville, espinacas con garbanzos is the dish of cuaresma (Lent) — the meat-free weeks when tavern cooks lean on chickpeas, greens, and that ancient bread-cumin-vinegar paste (a technique carried through centuries of Andalusian kitchens). It is now a year-round tapas-bar staple, and autumn is when the spinach is at its best.

recipes.name: Aceitunas Aliñadas
recipes.seasonWhy: The Spanish table-olive verdeo (early green) harvest begins in September — and Andalusia grows roughly four out of every five of Spain's table olives, so September is when families and bars dress the year's first olives.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: A natural lunchbox or after-school snack — just use pitted olives for small kids.

groups.title: Marinade (one bowl, layered into the jar)
items: 500 g green table olives (aceitunas) — verdial or gordal varieties are classic, pitted or unpitted
Zest strips of 1 orange (naranja) and 1 lemon (limón) — thin strips of the colored peel only, no white pith
4 garlic cloves (dientes de ajo), lightly smashed
2 sprigs fresh thyme (tomillo), or 1 tsp dried

method: Place the olives in a clean glass jar or bowl.
Add the orange and lemon zest strips, smashed garlic, thyme, fennel seeds, bay leaf, and oregano (and paprika, if using).
Pour over the olive oil and sherry vinegar; sprinkle with the salt. Toss everything together so the olives are evenly coated.
Cover and refrigerate. Marinate at least 24 hours (up to 3 days), shaking or tossing once a day.
Bring to room temperature before serving; serve in a small bowl with a spoonful of the marinade drizzled over.
recipes.story: Andalusia grows roughly four out of every five of Spain's table olives, and the verdeo (green-harvest) season opens in September — exactly when families and bars dress the year's first olives with orange peel, fennel, and thyme for the pre-dinner vermouth ritual. Marinated olives are the first thing set on a tapas-bar counter; they are the opening note of Andalusian eating.

recipes.name: Spring Pea, Asparagus & Broad Bean Risotto with Lemon & Mint
recipes.seasonWhy: Victoria spring = Sep–Nov; the Koo Wee Rup–Dalmore asparagus harvest typically starts in September, fresh peas are abundant in spring, and broad beans are widely available at spring farmers' markets.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Naturally kid-friendly: creamy rice and sweet peas. Omit the wine (use stock) and chop the asparagus small, cooking it until fully tender for under-5s.

groups.title: Broth
items: 1.25 L (5 cups) vegetable stock — keep at a bare simmer in a saucepan throughout

groups.title: Aromatics + rice
items: ½ cup dry white wine (optional — replace with extra stock)

groups.title: Spring vegetables (added late so they stay green)
items: 1 bunch asparagus (~250 g), woody ends snapped off, spears cut into 3 cm pieces
1½ cups fresh spring peas (shelled) or frozen peas, thawed
1 cup broad beans, podded and peeled
Reserved asparagus tips (a few, blanched 2 min, for garnish)

groups.title: Finish
items: ⅓ cup torn fresh mint leaves
80 g Meredith goat's cheese (tangy soft goat's cheese from Victoria), crumbled
Sea salt and cracked black pepper

method: Keep the stock at a bare simmer in a saucepan. In a large heavy pan, heat the olive oil over medium heat; soften the onion 4–5 min until translucent, then stir in the garlic for 30 seconds.
Add the arborio rice and toast 1–2 min, stirring, until the grains are glossy with translucent edges.
Pour in the wine (if using) and stir until absorbed. Then add the warm stock one ladle at a time, stirring often and letting each addition absorb before the next — about 18 min total.
When the rice is nearly al dente (about 5 min of stock left to go), stir in the asparagus pieces, peas, and broad beans. Continue ladling stock until the rice is creamy and just tender.
Take off the heat. Beat in the cold butter, parmesan, lemon zest and juice until glossy. Season boldly with salt and pepper. Rest 2 min with the lid on.
Spoon into warm bowls, scatter with mint, crumbled goat's cheese, and the reserved asparagus tips. Finish with a thread of olive oil.
recipes.story: The Koo Wee Rup–Dalmore region southeast of Melbourne grows roughly 93% of Australia's asparagus; the main harvest runs mid-August to mid-December, typically starting in September. In ideal spring conditions spears can grow 1–2 cm in an hour — growers harvest in the cool of the night so the tender spears don't cook in the field. Risotto is an Italian technique, but this green version is the dish Victorian cooks make to mark the first spears of the season: spring on a plate.

sources.name: wineselectors.com.au — Manu Feildel pea & asparagus risotto

recipes.name: Bush Damper with Lemon Myrtle Butter
recipes.seasonWhy: Evergreen traditional staple — a bread, not a seasonal crop; spring campfire/picnic season makes it timely.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: A natural after-school snack — serve warm torn wedges with golden syrup or jam alongside the lemon myrtle butter (kids may prefer plain butter or honey, since the myrtle butter is strong).

groups.title: The liquid
items: ½ cup water (plus a splash more if the dough is dry)

groups.title: Lemon myrtle butter (whipped while the damper bakes)
items: ½ tsp dried ground lemon myrtle (or 1 tsp fresh, very finely chopped)

method: Heat the oven to 180°C (350°F). Lightly flour a baking tray.
Rub the cold butter into the flour and salt with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs.
Make a well in the centre; pour in the milk and water and mix with a wooden spoon (or your hands) to a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead gently for 1–2 min on a floured surface — don't overwork it.
Shape into a round loaf about 20 cm across. Slash a deep cross on top with a sharp knife (the traditional damper mark, and it helps the loaf cook through).

Bake 40–50 min until deep golden and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped underneath. (Traditionally it was buried in campfire ashes with the fire damped down — an oven or camp oven does the same job at home.)
Meanwhile, beat the soft butter with the lemon myrtle and salt until pale and fluffy.
Cool the damper on a wire rack for 10 min, tear it open while warm, and spread thickly with lemon myrtle butter.
recipes.story: Damper was first mentioned in print in 1825, in memoirs edited by Barron Field, judge of the Supreme Court of NSW. The name likely comes either from a Lancashire expression meaning "something that damps the appetite" or from the cook's trick of damping down the campfire and burying the dough in the hot ashes. It became the staple of swagmen, drovers, and stockmen because flour and salt were easy to carry and all it needed was water. In 1946 the Sydney Morning Herald printed Bill Beatty's bush recipe: a pound of flour, water, a pinch of salt, kneaded long and cooked in a foot of hot ashes. Lemon myrtle adds the native twist: an Australian rainforest leaf dubbed the "queen of the herbs," with more citral than lemon itself.

recipes.name: Vegetarian Mapo Tofu
recipes.seasonWhy: Autumn in Sichuan = fresh tofu, late-summer shiitake, autumn green scallions; the Sichuan autumn harvest table centers on warming mala dishes as nights cool.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Halve the doubanjiang and skip the chili flakes/oil; keep the Sichuan-pepper garnish on the side so grown-ups add it. Kids love the glossy red sauce on rice.

groups.title: Tofu (goes in last)
items: 400 g (1 block) medium-soft tofu, cut into 2 cm cubes

groups.title: Mushroom "mince" (fried first, replaces the ground pork)
items: 6–8 dried shiitake mushrooms, soaked 30 min in warm water, squeezed dry and finely minced (reserve the soaking liquid)

groups.title: Aromatics (the flavor base)
items: 2 scallions — whites minced (greens chopped for garnish)
1½ tbsp doubanjiang (Pixian fermented chili-bean paste — check label: no meat/fish)
1 tbsp douchi (fermented black beans), lightly rinsed and chopped
1 tsp chili powder or dried chili flakes (optional, for extra heat)

groups.title: Braising liquid + finishing
items: 1½ cups water or the reserved mushroom soaking liquid
1½ tsp cornstarch mixed with 3 tbsp cold water (slurry)
1–2 tsp ground Sichuan peppercorns, toasted and ground

method: Blanch tofu cubes in lightly salted boiling water 2–3 minutes (firms them so they don't break). Drain and set aside.
Heat a dry pan and toast the Sichuan peppercorns until fragrant and slightly darker; grind to a powder. Set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp oil in a wok over medium-high. Fry the mushroom mince until golden and slightly crisp, 5–6 minutes. Remove.

Same wok: 2 tbsp oil, medium heat. Add ginger, garlic, scallion whites; sauté 20 seconds. Add doubanjiang and douchi; fry until the oil turns brick-red and smells deeply fragrant (~2 min). Add chili flakes if using.
Deglaze with Shaoxing wine. Pour in the mushroom soaking liquid (or water). Stir in soy sauce and sugar.
Slide in the tofu cubes and the browned mushroom mince. Simmer gently 5 minutes so the tofu absorbs the sauce.
Drizzle in the cornstarch slurry, stirring gently, until the sauce thickens and clings.
Finish with sesame oil and half the ground Sichuan pepper. Plate, dust with remaining pepper, scatter scallion greens. Serve over steamed jasmine rice.
recipes.story: In the 1860s in Chengdu, a woman everyone called Chen Mapo ("Pockmarked Grandmother Chen") ran a tiny tofu shop near a busy dock. Porters and oil haulers would stop in for her tofu simmered with the fiery chili-bean paste of her kitchen. The dish was so famous it took her name — Mapo Tofu. On Mid-Autumn night, Chinese families across the world sit down to reunion dinners under the full moon, and this is exactly the kind of loud, numbing-spicy, everybody-at-the-table dish that belongs there.

recipes.name: Osmanthus Steamed Rice Cake (Guihua Gao)
recipes.seasonWhy: Sweet-scented osmanthus flowers bloom only in September–October — this snack is literally a taste of right now, and osmanthus pairs with the Mid-Autumn full moon in Chinese poetry and folklore.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: It's already perfect — sweet, bouncy, honey-fragrant. Cut into fun squares and let kids scatter the dried flowers on top before steaming.

groups.title: Osmanthus syrup (made first, cools while you mix)
items: 2 tbsp dried osmanthus flowers (sweet-scented osmanthus blossoms)

groups.title: Batter (mixed second)
items: A few extra dried osmanthus flowers, for the top

method: Syrup: simmer water + rock sugar until fully dissolved. Off the heat, stir in the dried osmanthus flowers and steep 10 minutes. Strain (or leave the flowers in for extra fragrance). Let cool.
Batter: whisk both flours in a bowl. Pour in the cooled osmanthus syrup (plus osmanthus honey if using) and whisk to a smooth, pourable batter — no lumps.
Oil a shallow heatproof dish or line a bamboo steamer with muslin. Pour batter no more than ~2 cm deep. Scatter a few dried osmanthus flowers on top.
Steam over high heat 20–25 minutes until set and springy (a skewer comes out clean).
Cool completely, then slice into small squares. Serve at room temperature with tea.
recipes.story: In September and October, the osmanthus trees of Sichuan bloom all at once and the whole street smells like peaches and apricots — the Chinese call it "fragrance you can taste." Old Chengdu families gather osmanthus blossoms, candy them in honey, and steam this jade-white cake to eat with tea while the full Mid-Autumn moon rises. The poet Li Qingzhao wrote that the moon and the osmanthus belong to each other — tonight they do.

recipes.name: Sichuan-Style Five-Kernel Mooncake
recipes.seasonWhy: Autumn nut harvest — walnuts, peanuts, sunflower and pumpkin kernels, sesame — all at their freshest in September; this is the Mid-Autumn Festival's signature sweet.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Reduce the Sichuan pepper powder to a pinch (or omit) for the kids' batch; let kids press the moulds — the flower patterns are the fun part. Serve 1 wedge with tea.

groups.title: Filling — dry mix (toasted first)
items: 25 g white sesame seeds + 15 g black sesame seeds

groups.title: Filling — binding paste (stirred in second)
items: 40 g sugared rose petals / rose sauce (tangmeigui)
1 tbsp neutral oil + 1 tsp toasted sesame oil
½ tsp ground Sichuan peppercorns (the Sichuan signature!)
60 g cooked glutinous rice flour (kao fen — dry-toast raw flour in a pan until lightly golden)
1–2 tbsp warm water, as needed to bind

groups.title: Crust (rested, then wraps the filling)
items: 1 tsp lye/alkaline water (jianshui) — skip if unavailable

method: Toast: spread all nuts, seeds, and sesame on a tray; bake 150°C / 300°F for 12–15 minutes until fragrant. Cool, then chop coarsely (keep texture — no powder).

Filling: combine the toasted mix + diced candied fruits in a bowl. Stir in rose sauce, syrup, oils, sugar, salt, and Sichuan pepper powder. Add the cooked glutinous rice flour gradually, tossing until everything binds into a pressable mass (drizzle warm water if dry). Divide into 65 g balls.
Crust: mix syrup, oil, and lye water; fold in the flour until just smooth. Cover and rest 2 hours at room temperature.
Wrap: divide crust into 35 g pieces. Flatten each into a disc, cup a filling ball, and seal fully (filling : crust ≈ 2 : 1).
Mould: dust a 100 g mooncake mould lightly with flour. Press each wrapped ball firmly into the mould and knock it out onto a lined tray.
Bake: 205°C / 400°F for 5 minutes to set the pattern. Remove, lightly mist or brush with water (no egg wash — egg-free), return at 165°C / 325°F for 15–20 minutes until golden. Cool completely.
Rest 2–3 days in a sealed container ("回油" — the crust softens and turns glossy). Slice into wedges and share — mooncakes are for cutting and passing around.
recipes.story: On Mid-Autumn night, the moon is the roundest of the year — and everything on the table goes round to match: pomelos, mooncakes, the whole family gathered in a circle. Sichuan makes its mooncakes the Sichuan way: a thin crisp crust around five kinds of nuts, candied winter melon, and — unmistakably — a breath of rose and Sichuan pepper. The round cake and the round moon wish the same thing: 团圆 (tuanyuan) — that everyone you love comes home whole.

recipes.name: Vegetarian Waterblommetjie Bredie
recipes.seasonWhy: Waterblommetjie (Cape water flower) seasonal window is June–September; late September is the tail of the season — fresh punnets still available at Cape markets, tinned flowers are a documented backup. (Do not claim peak season.)

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Omit the chilli entirely; add 1 extra potato cut smaller so it nearly melts into the stew; serve as "flower stew" over rice — kids love spotting the tiny white flowers. Start with half a lemon for little palates.

groups.title: Morning prep (first entry)
items: 800 g–1 kg fresh waterblommetjies (Cape water flowers; 2 punnets; or 2 × 140 g tins, drained)
Cold water + 2 Tbsp salt, for soaking

groups.title: Pot entry 1 — hard aromatics
items: 1 small green chilli, slit (optional; omit for kids)

groups.title: Pot entry 2 — hard vegetables
items: 500 g potatoes, peeled and cut into chunky blocks
250 g brown mushrooms, quartered (meaty body of the stew)

groups.title: Pot entry 3 — delicate finish
items: Juice of 1 lemon + a little zest (or a handful of suring [wild sorrel], well washed and chopped — the traditional Cape souring herb)

method: Morning: trim stalks and browned edges from the flowers, wash well, and soak in cold salted water for at least 3 hours (or overnight). Rinse thoroughly, swirl to dislodge grit, drain.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot. Fry the onions with the cloves until translucent and golden at the edges. Add garlic, crushed coriander seeds and chilli; stir 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the potatoes and mushrooms, toss to coat. Pour in the vegetable stock, cover, and simmer gently 25–30 minutes until the potatoes are nearly tender.
Add the drained waterblommetjies, stir through, cover and simmer 15–20 minutes more — done when the flowers still have a soft crunch, "resembling miniature artichoke leaves". Don't overcook.
Stir in the lemon juice and zest (or suring), nutmeg, salt and pepper. Rest 10 minutes off the heat. Serve over steamed rice with parsley.
recipes.story: Waterblommetjies were gathered and eaten by the indigenous Khoikhoi long before Jan van Riebeeck arrived in 1652; early settlers and their enslaved workers learnt from the Khoikhoi that these pond flowers were edible. The dish is a three-culture fusion: the Dutch slow-stewing method, the spices of enslaved people from the East, and the indigenous Khoisan ingredient. It remains the Boland's beloved late-winter/early-spring ritual, celebrated at the annual Waterblommetjie Festival.

recipes.name: Cape Malay Potato & Pea Samoosas
recipes.seasonWhy: Peas are a spring vegetable (Sep–Nov per Crush chart); potatoes, onions, garlic are year-round staples.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Skip the chillies completely; make the triangles smaller (bite-size, 25–30 minis) so little hands can hold them — the filling is already mild and sweet from the peas. Lighter version: brush with oil and bake at 200°C for 18–20 minutes instead of frying.

groups.title: Pastry (egg-free — make first, rests while filling cooks)
items: (Rub oil into flour + salt until crumbly; add water a little at a time and knead 8–10 minutes to a stiff, smooth dough; oil lightly, cover, rest 30 minutes.)

groups.title: Sealing paste (egg-free fix)
items: 3 Tbsp flour whisked smooth with 3–4 Tbsp water

groups.title: Pot entry 1 — hard aromatics
items: 2–3 small green chillies, crushed (or 1 tsp crushed dried chillies; omit for kids)

groups.title: Pot entry 2 — hard vegetables
items: 500 g potatoes, peeled and cut into small cubes, parboiled 5 minutes and drained

groups.title: Pot entry 3 — soft finish
items: 100 g fresh or frozen peas (spring peas!)

groups.title: Mint-coriander yoghurt dip (optional)
items: ½ cup plain yoghurt + ½ cup mint leaves + 2 Tbsp coriander + 1 tsp lemon juice + pinch of salt, blended smooth

method: Make pastry; rest 30 min.
Braise the onion in oil until deep golden (5–10 min). Add whole jeera and koljana; let them sizzle 30 seconds. Add chillies, ginger, garlic; cook 1 minute.

Add the parboiled potato cubes and turmeric with a splash of water; cook, stirring, until the potatoes are soft and the mixture is dry (the Cape Malay rule: the filling must be dry so the pastry stays crisp). Stir in the peas and cook 5 minutes. Cool completely, then fold in coriander and lemon juice.

Divide dough into 10 balls; roll each into a thin circle, cut in half. Form each half into a cone, seal the seam with flour paste, fill with a spoonful of filling, seal the top. Keep covered with a damp cloth so the pastry doesn't dry.
Fry in medium-hot oil (170–180°C) in batches, turning, until deep golden and crisp, 4–5 minutes. Drain on paper towel. Serve hot with the mint yoghurt dip or atjar (Cape pickle relish).
recipes.story: The samosa arrived in India as the sambosa with Arab traders in the 13th–14th centuries, then travelled to the Cape with enslaved people shipped from the East Indies by the Dutch. In the Bo-Kaap it became the samoosa — smaller and more delicate than its Indian cousin — folded by hand into triangles, a staple of Cape Malay tables alongside koesisters and daltjies. Potato-and-pea is one of the classic vegetarian fillings, folded in batches for Ramadan evenings and family gatherings.

recipes.name: Tom Kha Hed
recipes.seasonWhy: Thailand's rainy (green) season runs Jun–Sep — late September is the tail of the rains; wild mushrooms are the defining rainy-season produce, foraged from the forests after continuous rains.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Naturally mild and creamy — keep the chilies whole or on the side so kids get the gentle version.

groups.title: Group 1 — aromatic simmer base (in first)
items: Galangal (kha — peppery, piney rhizome) — 3-inch piece, thinly sliced
Lemongrass (takhrai) — 2 stalks, bruised, cut into 2-inch pieces
Thai bird's eye chilies (phrik khi nu) — 3–4, lightly crushed (optional; leave whole for a milder soup)

groups.title: Group 2 — vegetables (in second)
items: Mixed mushrooms (hed) — 400 g, halved or sliced: straw mushrooms, oyster mushrooms, shiitake (use wild rainy-season mushrooms such as hed thop if available)

groups.title: Group 3 — finishing (in last, mostly off the heat)
items: Thick coconut cream (hua kati — first-press coconut cream) — 1 cup (250 ml)
Garnish: coriander leaves (phak chi), sliced spring onions (ton hom)

method: Pour the thin coconut milk into a pot; add galangal, lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves, and chilies. Bring to a gentle simmer (never a hard boil — coconut milk splits) and simmer 5 minutes until fragrant.
Add mushrooms, cabbage, and tomato. Simmer 5–7 minutes until the mushrooms are tender.
Stir in the thick coconut cream; warm through for 1 minute.
Off the heat, season: lime juice, light soy sauce, palm sugar, salt — balance the Thai sour-salty-sweet triangle to taste.
Ladle into bowls; garnish with coriander and spring onion. Serve with steamed jasmine rice.
recipes.story: In Thailand's green season the rains wake the forests and wild mushrooms — hed thop, termite mushrooms — push through the soil. Foragers head out before dawn and the morning markets fill with baskets of them. Tom kha hed tastes like that season: a galangal-lemongrass broth, coconut, and a tangle of mushrooms.

recipes.name: Khanom Krok
recipes.seasonWhy: Late rainy season = sweet corn and young coconut at their best in Thai markets; khanom krok is the classic Thai market snack, cooked to order in cast-iron dimpled pans.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: A natural kid favorite: bite-size, sweet-salty, crisp outside and custardy inside.

groups.title: Group 1 — crisp shell batter (blend first)
items: Cooked jasmine rice — ¼ cup (the traditional crispness trick)
Oil — 1 tbsp, plus more for greasing the pan

groups.title: Group 2 — custard filling (whisk second)
items: Thick coconut cream (hua kati — first-press coconut cream) — 1 cup

groups.title: Group 3 — toppings (sprinkle last)
items: Sweet corn kernels (khao phot), cooked — ½ cup
Taro (pheuak), steamed and diced — ¼ cup
Scallions (ton hom), thinly sliced — 2 tbsp (savory option)

method: Blend the shell-batter ingredients until completely smooth — thin, like crepe batter. Rest 10 minutes.
Whisk the filling ingredients until no lumps remain; it should be noticeably thicker than the shell batter.
Heat a khanom krok pan (an aebleskiver / takoyaki / paniyaram pan works) over medium heat and oil each cup well — the batter must sizzle on contact.
Pour shell batter ⅔ full into each cup; swirl gently so it coats the walls.
After ~1 minute, spoon filling into the center of each; sprinkle with toppings.
Cover with a lid and cook 3–6 minutes, until the edges are golden-crisp and the center is set but still soft and custardy.
Lift out with a small spoon; serve in pairs, hot.
recipes.story: Sold from bicycle carts and market stalls across Thailand, khanom krok is cooked to order in a cast-iron pan full of dimples — crisp shell outside, molten coconut custard inside, always served in pairs. The sizzle when the batter hits the hot pan is the sound of a Thai morning market.

recipes.name: Humita en chala
recipes.seasonWhy: Early spring in the Northwest is NOT fresh-choclo season (maíz is sown in September, harvested in summer); the recipe uses frozen choclo kernels and keeps the traditional chalas (corn husks) for wrapping. Onion, morrón, basil and queso criollo are all available now.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Natural — the filling is a soft, sweet corn pudding. For kids: skip the ají molido, double the cheese square, and make mini humitas (half size).

groups.title: Husks (wrap)
items: 12–14 fresh ears of choclo (tender white corn) — if fresh with good husks is available, reserve the largest inner husks; otherwise 1.2 kg frozen choclo kernels + dried corn husks (chalas secas, rehydrated in hot water)

groups.title: Sofrito (into the hot oil first)
items: 1 red bell pepper (morrón rojo), finely diced
3 tbsp neutral oil (traditional versions sometimes use beef tallow — oil keeps it vegetarian)
½ tsp ají molido (ground chili) — omit for kids

groups.title: Corn body
items: 1.2 kg grated or processed choclo kernels (grated = traditional texture)

groups.title: Cheese core
items: 300 g queso criollo salteño (Salta creole cheese), or goat cheese / firm mozzarella, sliced into small squares — one square per humita

method: Prep the chalas: peel husks from fresh ears without tearing; wash and soak in hot water 10 min to soften. If using dried husks, rehydrate in hot water.
Grate the corn: grate kernels (or pulse in a food processor to a creamy coarse texture; strain off excess liquid if very wet).
Sofrito: heat oil, sauté onion + morrón until translucent (7–8 min). Stir in pimentón, ají molido, salt.
Corn body: add grated corn, milk, and torn basil to the sofrito. Cook on low 15 min, stirring, until thick and creamy. Taste for salt. Let cool slightly.
Wrap: cross two chalas, spoon 2–3 tbsp filling into the center, place one cheese square on top, fold into a square parcel, tie with strips of chala.
Steam: line the pot bottom with the leftover cobs (keeps parcels off the base), add parcels, cover with salted boiling water, and simmer 1 hour.
Serve hot, in the chala — guests unwrap at the table.
recipes.story: Humita's name comes from the Quechua "huminta" — this is pre-Columbian cooking: corn, ground on stone, steamed in its own leaves. In Salta it is the dish of Semana Santa (Holy Week), when families gather to grate dozens of choclos and wrap hundreds of little parcels together — unwrapping a hot humita at the table is half the ritual.
