recipes.name: Quesillo con dulce de cayote y nueces
recipes.seasonWhy: Cayote is an autumn/winter harvest that stores for months; the dulce is a pantry preserve — genuinely available and traditional in early spring. Walnuts and quesillo are year-round.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Natural — kids love sweet cheese + jam. For kids: serve the dulce over quesillo in a small bowl with a spoon; it is already mild, nothing to change.

groups.title: Dulce (jam — into the pot first)
items: 1 kg cayote pulp (fig-leaf gourd, Cucurbita ficifolia — looks like a watermelon outside; from ~1 medium cayote, ~1.5 kg whole)
500 g sugar (half the weight of the peeled, seeded pulp)
Zest of 1 lemon (optional, adds a bright note — traditionalists use it)

groups.title: To serve
items: 400 g quesillo salteño (Salta stretched-curd cheese; or fresh mozzarella / queso de cabra), sliced

method: Open the cayote: warm the whole cayote in a moderate oven 10 min — the heat loosens the tough skin. Tap with a rolling pin and peel it off easily.
Shred by hand: scoop out the seeds, then pull the pulp into threads with your fingers, never a knife — the fibers are the whole point of this jam.
Macerate: toss the fibers with the sugar in a glass bowl, cover, and rest overnight (~10 hours). The fruit releases its own juice — no water added, ever.

Slow cook: transfer to a heavy pot (copper if you have it), add the clove and lemon zest, and cook on the lowest heat, stirring with a wooden spoon, until the fibers turn translucent amber and the syrup thickens enough that a spoon dragged across the pot bottom leaves a trail. About 1–1.5 hours.
Jar: cool and keep in glass jars (keeps weeks refrigerated).
Plate: lay quesillo slices on a plate, spoon warm dulce de cayote over them, scatter the walnuts on top.
recipes.story: Cayote is one of the Northwest's heritage foods — a gourd whose pulp naturally shreds into silk-like threads, made into jam since colonial times. Paired with quesillo, the hand-stretched cheese of the Valles Calchaquíes, it is the dessert plate of Salta and Jujuy: sweet fibers, salty cheese, crunchy walnuts. The same dulce fills the region's famous empanadillas de cayote.

sources.name: El Arte de Amasar — Quesillo con dulce de cayote y nueces
Prensa Mercosur — dulce de cayote master notes

recipes.name: Phở Chay
recipes.seasonWhy: Late September = tail of the rainy season (monsoon May–Oct); fresh herbs, mushrooms, and leafy greens abundant; the northern early-autumn rice harvest is underway.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Serve a milder bowl — fewer chilies, shorter noodle lengths for little hands, extra tofu cubes, lime only. No separate recipe needed, just assembly tweaks.

groups.title: Broth vegetables (simmer first)
items: 1 large yellow onion, halved (char on open flame or under broiler until blackened in spots)
4-inch piece ginger (gừng), sliced and charred alongside the onion
1 small daikon (củ cải trắng), peeled, cut into chunks
¼ head green cabbage or Napa cabbage, roughly chopped
1 apple or Asian pear, quartered (natural sweetness)

groups.title: Spice blend (dry-toast, then bag in cheesecloth)
Broth seasoning (added after straining)
items: 2 tbsp mushroom seasoning powder or vegetarian fish sauce (nước mắm chay)

groups.title: Bowls
items: 400 g (14 oz) dried flat rice noodles (bánh phở)
300 g firm tofu (đậu hũ), cut in slabs and pan-seared golden
200 g mixed mushrooms — shiitake caps + king oyster (nấm đùi gà), sliced and sautéed

groups.title: Herb plate (đĩa rau thơm) — at the table
items: Thai basil (húng quế), culantro (ngò gai), cilantro (ngò rí)
Bean sprouts (giá đỗ), thinly sliced white onion
Lime (chanh) wedges, sliced bird's-eye chilies (ớt hiểm), scallion greens

method: Char the onion and ginger until blackened in spots; rinse off loose char.
Dry-toast the spice blend 2–3 minutes until fragrant; tie in cheesecloth.
Simmer broth vegetables + charred aromatics in water 30 min; add the spice bag for the last 15 min. Strain, pressing solids gently. (Optional: return reserved shiitake and daikon to the broth.)
Season the clear broth with rock sugar, salt, and mushroom seasoning / nước mắm chay to taste; keep at a bare simmer.
Blanch bánh phở until just tender; rinse in cool water. Sear tofu slabs; sauté mushrooms until browned. Blanch bok choy 1 min.
Assemble: noodles in deep bowls, tofu, mushrooms, bok choy; ladle over steaming broth. Serve with the herb plate — everyone finishes their own bowl.
recipes.story: Phở chay was born in Vietnam's Buddhist vegetarian kitchens: on the full and new moon each lunar month, temples and chay restaurants in Huế and Saigon ladle out this spice-perfumed noodle soup. All the ceremony of phở — charred aromatics, toasted spice, a tableside herb plate — with a broth built entirely from vegetables, fruit, and mushrooms.

recipes.name: Bánh Cuốn Chay
recipes.seasonWhy: Late September = tail of the rainy season (monsoon May–Oct); fresh herbs, mushrooms, and leafy greens abundant.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Plain unfilled rolls (kids love the pan-rolling theatre) with a mild sweet-soy dip and cucumber ribbons.

groups.title: Filling (sauté in order)
items: 50 g dried wood ear mushrooms (mộc nhĩ), soaked and finely chopped — goes in first
150 g fried tofu (đậu hũ chiên), sliced thin
1 tbsp white part of leek (hành boaro phần trắng), minced
Seasoning: 1 tbsp soy sauce (nước tương), 1 tsp vegetarian stock powder, salt and black pepper to taste

groups.title: Dipping sauce — nước chấm chay
items: 1 tsp soy sauce, 1 tsp lime juice

groups.title: To finish
items: Scallion oil (mỡ hành) — sliced scallions wilted in hot oil
Cucumber (dưa leo) ribbons, blanched bean sprouts, fresh herbs, crushed roasted peanuts (đậu phộng rang)

method: Whisk batter smooth; rest 30 min–2 hr (stir before each use).
Sauté filling: leek in oil until golden; add wood ear, carrot, jicama — cook until crisp-tender; add tofu and seasonings; finish with pepper.
Steam the sheets: brush a nonstick skillet with a whisper of oil over medium heat; ladle in batter, swirl thin, cover 15–20 seconds until translucent; slide out onto an oiled plate.
Place filling down the center of each sheet and roll. Repeat until batter is used (~16 rolls).
Plate rolls with a drizzle of scallion oil, crispy shallots, cucumber, bean sprouts, herbs, and peanuts. Serve with nước chấm chay.
recipes.story: At dawn in Hanoi, bánh cuốn vendors spread rice batter paper-thin over a cloth stretched above a steamer, lift each translucent sheet in seconds, and roll it around wood ear mushrooms and tofu. On vegetarian-eating days the same stalls serve bánh cuốn chay — the full street-food theatre, no meat involved.

sources.name: Cookpad Vietnam / Hai Thuy Tran — bánh cuốn chay đổ chảo
Helen's Recipes — vegetarian steamed rice rolls

recipes.name: Porotos Granados
recipes.seasonWhy: Classically a late-summer harvest dish, cooked year-round from dried beans; zapallo stores months post-harvest, frozen choclo works outside summer, and fresh albahaca returns in October.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Everyday Chilean family food, routinely served to children — for kids omit the ají de color dusting and keep seasoning mild; the mazamorra (ground-corn) version is smoother for small kids.

groups.title: Pot-entry group 1 (the long simmer — beans first)
items: 500 g (2½ cups) dried porotos granados (mature cranberry beans) — look for pale beans with red streaks; soak overnight 8–12 h, drain

groups.title: Pot-entry group 2 (added once beans are nearly tender)
items: 400 g zapallo (pumpkin/winter squash, the sweet Chilean variety), peeled, cut into medium cubes
1½ cups choclo (fresh corn) kernels — frozen is fine outside summer
1 cup choclo ground to a coarse paste (the mazamorra variation — this paste thickens the stew)

groups.title: Sofrito (cooked separately, stirred in at the end)
items: 1 tsp ají de color (Chilean smoked-chili powder; sweet-paprika style) — for the red color
1 cup fresh albahaca (basil) leaves, finely chopped (reserve a few whole leaves for garnish)
Salt and black pepper to taste

method: Beans in a large pot with 12 cups fresh water. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then simmer half-covered 45–60 min until almost tender. (Pressure cooker: 20 min after pressure.)

Add the zapallo cubes and both portions of choclo (whole kernels + ground paste). Simmer 20–25 min, stirring now and then so the ground corn doesn't stick, until the zapallo is soft and breaking down — this is what makes the stew creamy. Season with salt.
Meanwhile make the sofrito: heat the oil, soften the onion 8–10 min until translucent, add garlic 1 min, then stir in ají de color, comino, and chopped albahaca; cook 1 min until fragrant.
Stir the sofrito into the bean pot. Simmer 10 min more so flavors marry. Mash a few beans against the pot wall for extra creaminess. Adjust salt and pepper.
Rest 5 min. Serve in deep bowls, garnished with whole albahaca leaves and a dusting of ají de color. Traditional accompaniment: sliced tomato or pebre (Chilean fresh tomato-cilantro salsa).
recipes.story: The name "porotos granados" comes from the ripeness of the beans in their pod — granado means plump/mature — and summer was the season families gathered in the Chilean countryside to desgranar (shell) beans together. It's the dish behind the saying "más chileno que los porotos" (more Chilean than beans): a University of Chile heritage project (La Gran Porotada) documents how deeply the bean is woven into Chilean identity, collecting citizen recipes from Arica to Punta Arenas.

recipes.name: Mote con Huesillos
recipes.seasonWhy: A documented spring classic — "perfecta para la época de primavera y verano" (Kitchen Center): late September's first warm weeks are exactly when Chile's streets reach for this cold refreshment.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: This is a non-alcoholic sweet drink Chilean kids buy from street carts; kids' adaptation: less syrup (dilute with water), fewer cloves.

groups.title: The syrup pot (huesillos first — they need the longest time)
items: 250 g huesillos (dried peaches with the pit left in — "little bones," hence the name)
100 g sugar + 75 g chancaca (unrefined cane sugar / piloncillo) — the chancaca gives the signature amber color
1 strip of orange peel (no white pith)

groups.title: The mote pot (separate pot)
items: 250 g mote (cooked wheat berries — husked wheat grains, sold ready to cook)

groups.title: To serve
items: 2 heaping tablespoons mote per glass + 2 huesillos + syrup to fill; serve very cold with a big spoon

method: Night before: rinse the huesillos, cover with the 1.5 L water, and soak overnight (minimum 3 h).

Syrup: tip the huesillos with their soaking water into a pot. Add chancaca, sugar, cinnamon, orange peel, cloves. Simmer gently 45–60 min until the peaches are plump and tender. Cool completely, then refrigerate at least 4 h (overnight is better) — the syrup deepens as it chills.

Mote: rinse mote under cold water, boil in a separate pot of unsalted water 30–45 min until the grains are tender but still chewy. Drain, cool, refrigerate (spoon a little cold syrup over it so it stays moist and picks up flavor).
Assembly: spoon mote into a tall glass, add 2 huesillos, fill with the cold syrup. Serve ice-cold with a spoon.
recipes.story: The motero (street wheat-seller) is one of Chile's oldest street professions, dating to colonial times: vendors carried baskets of mote on their heads with their jars and spoons and sold it by the cuartillo — historical accounts record "tres centavos el cuartillo." Moteros and huesillo sellers eventually merged into the single iconic street drink. In the 1950s–60s there was a boom of mote-con-huesillo cart vendors; formal health permits only came in 1978. Pablo de Rokha reportedly chose a glass of jugo con huesillos as his final meal.

recipes.name: Moi Moi
recipes.seasonWhy: Wet season May–Oct; October = tail of the wet season. Plantain is a year-round staple of southwestern Nigeria, plentiful in the wet season; black-eyed peas / honey beans are everyday Nigerian staples.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Make a mild batch (1/2 scotch bonnet, kid-size leaf parcels); sweet dodo is a natural kid-pleaser.

groups.title: A. Bean base (first in — blended)
items: 2 cups dried black-eyed peas (cowpeas; also called honey beans / ewa oloyin)
2 scotch bonnet peppers (atarodo) — reduce to 1 for a milder pudding

groups.title: C. For wrapping
items: Fresh banana leaves or ewe eran (Thaumatococcus daniellii) leaves (traditional), or heat-safe ramekins / foil pouches

groups.title: D. Dodo (fried sweet plantain — served alongside)
items: 2 ripe (yellow with black spots) plantains, sliced diagonally

method: Soak the beans 4 hours or overnight; rub off the skins and rinse until clean.
Blend the peeled beans with tatashe, scotch bonnet, onion and just enough water to a smooth, creamy paste (like light cake batter).
Turn into a bowl; stir in the red palm oil, crumbled stock cubes and salt until evenly combined. Thin with a splash of hot water if too thick.
Wilt the banana leaves briefly over a flame (or rinse the ramekins). Scoop the batter in (fill 3/4), fold and tie the leaves or cover the ramekins with foil.
Set the parcels upright in a pot lined with leftover leaves or a steaming rack; add 1 inch of water, cover tightly and steam 45–60 minutes. A knife inserted comes out clean when done.
Dodo: heat oil, fry the plantain slices until golden on both sides; drain, salt lightly. Serve beside the moi moi.
recipes.story: Moi moi is a protein-rich Yoruba classic — street food, party (owambe) staple and breakfast plate all in one, traditionally steamed in ewe eran leaves folded into cone parcels. Peel-and-blend is the labor; the steam does the rest.

recipes.name: Boli
recipes.seasonWhy: Wet season May–Oct; plantain is the everyday southwestern staple.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Naturally mild and kid-friendly (roasted, not fried); serve plain or with groundnuts.

groups.title: A. On the grill
items: 3 semi-ripe plantains (yellow with a little black — too ripe goes mushy)

groups.title: B. Served alongside
items: Optional: quick pepper sauce — blended tatashe (red bell pepper) + onion + a little palm oil, simmered 10 min (fully vegetarian; no fish)

method: Wash the plantains; slit one side and peel.
Rub with salt and brush lightly with oil.
Charcoal grill or oven grill at ~200°C: roast 15–20 minutes, turning often, until golden with dark char marks and soft inside.
Serve hot with roasted groundnuts (the classic pairing) or the pepper sauce.
recipes.story: Boli is a Nigerian street-food icon — roadside vendors fanning charcoal in Lagos, Port Harcourt and Ibadan; students' favorite, "no class, just pure enjoyment." Traditionally eaten with roasted groundnuts.

recipes.name: Kabocha no Nimono
recipes.region: Japan — Miyazaki Prefecture (Miyazaki City), regional version
recipes.seasonWhy: Kabocha is strongly associated with Japanese autumn cooking; Japanese seasonal-cooking sources specifically identify kabocha no nimono as an autumn dish. Although kabocha is harvested in summer, it develops greater sweetness after storage and reaches particularly good eating quality around October–December.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES, provided vegetarian dashi is used. The Miyazaki regional recipe itself uses pumpkin, water and plant-based seasonings and contains no meat or fish. For a generic Japanese version, ordinary dashi may contain bonito, so kombu/shiitake or vegetable dashi should be explicitly specified.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: The Miyazaki regional version is served on elementary- and middle-school menus. For a children's serving, keep the kabocha soft and use the less salty end of the seasoning range; its naturally sweet, soft flesh is approachable without needing a separate “kids recipe.”

groups.title: Vegetarian adaptation, 4 servings
items: 3 cups / 720 ml vegetarian dashi (kombu-shiitake dashi or vegetable stock)

method: Wash the kabocha and scoop out the seeds and fibrous center.
Cut into roughly 3-inch / 7–8 cm pieces. Carefully trim away sharp corners; the skin can remain on.
Bring the vegetarian dashi to a boil in a wide pot.
Add the kabocha, cover, and simmer over medium heat for about 20–30 minutes, until tender when pierced with a fork.
Add the sugar, soy sauce, sake and salt.
Reduce the heat and cook another 15–20 minutes, allowing some of the broth to reduce and season the squash.
Turn off the heat and let the kabocha rest covered for several minutes. As it cools, it absorbs more of the seasoned broth.
Serve warm or at room temperature.
recipes.story: Kabocha has an interesting “second season”: Japanese Cooking 101 notes that freshly harvested kabocha is starchier and less sweet, but two to three months of storage allows moisture to decrease and starches to convert into sugars. That's one reason a squash harvested earlier can become particularly delicious in the autumn months. The Miyazaki Kurokawa variety has an even more distinctive history: the region's first pumpkin cultivation dates to 1907, while a black-skinned variety introduced from Chiba in 1924 eventually became a local specialty.

sources.name: Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries — Hyuuga Kurokawa Kabocha No Nimono
Just One Cookbook — Classic Japanese Fall Recipes

recipes.name: Hobakjuk
recipes.region: Korea (Chungcheongbuk-do, per Korean Traditional Local Food record)
recipes.seasonWhy: Korean sources describe hobakjuk as a fall-and-winter comfort food; Maangchi recalls her grandmother harvesting Korean pumpkins in fall and storing them for later use in hobakjuk — a harvest → storage → cool-weather porridge pattern.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES. The basic recipe consists of squash, sweet rice flour, water, sugar and salt; the optional rice balls and plant-based garnishes are also vegetarian.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Serve the smooth pumpkin porridge slightly warm, use 2 Tbsp sugar initially and adjust to taste, and omit nuts/garnishes for younger children. A Korean recipe source describes the dish as soft enough for children and older people — naturally mild, smooth and sweet.

groups.title: Simple vegetarian version, about 6 servings
items: 3¾ lb / 1.7 kg kabocha, Korean pumpkin or butternut squash, unpeeled weight
¼ cup / about 40 g sweet rice flour (glutinous rice flour)
3 Tbsp water, for the flour slurry

groups.title: Optional garnishes
items: cooked red beans, pine nuts, pumpkin seeds or jujubes

method: Cut the squash into quarters and remove the seeds and stringy interior.
Steam the squash until completely tender. Cool enough to handle, then remove the skin and cut the flesh into chunks.
Blend the cooked squash with the 3 cups water, sugar and salt until smooth.
Pour the mixture into a saucepan and bring to a gentle boil. Cook for about 10 minutes, stirring periodically.
Mix the ¼ cup sweet rice flour with 3 Tbsp water to make a smooth slurry.
Slowly pour the slurry into the pumpkin mixture while stirring continuously so it doesn't form lumps.
Reduce the heat and simmer for about 3 minutes, until the porridge thickens.
If using rice-cake balls, make them separately from sweet rice flour, salt and hot water; boil them until they float, then add them to the porridge.
Serve warm or chilled, with optional red beans, pine nuts, pumpkin seeds or jujube.
recipes.story: The dish has a beautiful preservation story: Maangchi describes her grandmother harvesting large Korean pumpkins in the fall and storing them in the pantry for winter, pulling one out whenever she wanted to make hobakjuk. There's also a neat linguistic detail: hobak is a broad Korean term covering pumpkin, squash and even some squash-like vegetables; danhobak, literally “sweet pumpkin,” is one of the varieties commonly used for hobakjuk.

sources.name: Korea Traditional Local Food — Hobak Juk

recipes.name: Parangikai Kootu
recipes.seasonWhy: Seasonal-library placement based on the pumpkin ingredient: October seasonal-produce guidance identifies pumpkin/winter squash as an autumn vegetable and specifically recommends pumpkin in kootu, curries, poriyal and dal preparations. The dish itself is usable year-round — “Autumn seasonal collection” ≠ “autumn-exclusive traditional dish.”
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES. The cited recipe contains pumpkin, moong dal, coconut, cumin and plant-based tempering ingredients, with no meat, fish or eggs.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: There isn't a distinct traditional children's parangikai kootu; the dish is naturally adaptable — make the coconut-cumin paste without chili, keep the pumpkin very soft, and mash some of the pumpkin and dal together before serving over rice. Record as “Kid-friendly adaptation: yes; established separate kid version: no.”

groups.title: 3–4 servings
items: 3 cups / about 450–500 g yellow pumpkin, peeled and cubed

groups.title: For tempering
items: 1 tsp neutral oil or coconut oil

method: Cook the moong dal until soft but not completely watery; set aside.
Peel and cube the pumpkin.
Put the pumpkin in a saucepan with enough water to almost cover it. Add turmeric and salt.
Cook until the pumpkin is soft but still holds its shape.
Grind the grated coconut and cumin seeds with a little water into a smooth or slightly coarse paste.
Add the cooked moong dal and coconut-cumin paste to the pumpkin.
Stir gently and simmer for about 2 minutes.
Heat the oil in a small pan.
Add mustard seeds and let them crackle. Add the urad dal, dried chili and curry leaves.
When the tempering is fragrant and the dal is lightly golden, pour it over the kootu.
Mix gently and serve hot with rice.
recipes.story: “Kootu” is less a single fixed recipe than a family of South Indian vegetable-and-lentil preparations. The vegetable can change while the basic idea remains: a vegetable is combined with dal and a coconut/spice mixture. And parangikai is particularly useful for a seasonal library because the same yellow pumpkin can move across the meal in very different forms — from savory kootu and sambar to sweets and halwa.

sources.name: Veg Recipes of India — South Indian Kootu background
October Seasonal Produce Guide — Indian Fall Cooking

recipes.name: Ribollita
recipes.seasonWhy: Ribollita is strongly associated with cool-weather Tuscan cooking, and contemporary Tuscan sources explicitly describe it as an autumn dish. Its ingredients also fit the season particularly well: beans, cavolo nero, root vegetables, tomatoes preserved from summer and sturdy stale bread.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES. The traditional versions cited here are vegetable-and-bean based. Some modern variations add meat or meat stock, so vegetable stock / bean cooking liquid should be specifically specified and meat additions omitted.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: An easy adaptation exists for children: use mild vegetable stock rather than strongly seasoned broth, omit the fennel seeds if their flavor is unfamiliar, chop the vegetables finely, cook until everything is very soft, mash some of the beans into the soup, and use small pieces of soft bread rather than large crusty pieces. The resulting soup is thick, mild and spoonable rather than brothy.

groups.title: 4 generous servings
items: 3 Tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to serve
½ loaf / about 250 g stale rustic or sourdough bread, torn into chunks
1 bunch cavolo nero, stalks removed and leaves shredded

method: Soak the cannellini beans overnight in plenty of cold water.
Drain them, place them in a large pot with one bay leaf, cover with fresh water and cook until tender.
Drain, reserving some of the cooking liquid.
Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot.
Add onion, carrot, celery and garlic. Cook gently until softened.
Add fennel seeds, thyme, tomatoes and the remaining bay leaf.
Add the cooked beans and enough bean-cooking water to make a thick soup.
Add the shredded cavolo nero and simmer until the greens are tender.
Stir in the stale bread. Let it soften and absorb the broth, producing the characteristic thick, almost stew-like consistency.
Season with salt and pepper.
Traditionally, the soup can be cooled and reheated again — the “reboiling” that gives ribollita its name.
Serve generously drizzled with extra-virgin olive oil.
recipes.story: Ribollita is essentially an early zero-waste recipe. Stale bread wasn't thrown away: it was added to leftover bean-and-vegetable soup, and the whole thing was reheated. The bread transforms the soup into something thick and filling. The name literally means “reboiled,” reflecting the traditional practice of reheating/reboiling leftover vegetable-and-bean soup with stale bread.

sources.name: The Guardian — How to make the perfect ribollita
The Guardian — Russell Norman's Tuscan ribollita

recipes.name: Goguma-bap
recipes.seasonWhy: Sweet potatoes are a classic autumn harvest ingredient, and the dish provides a particularly good example of how a seasonal crop can become an ordinary staple meal, rather than a special-occasion dish. The autumn connection is therefore ingredient- and harvest-based rather than a claim that goguma-bap is eaten only in autumn.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES. Maangchi explicitly categorizes goguma-bap as vegetarian, and identifies it as an easy, non-spicy, vegetarian one-bowl meal.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: The base recipe is already non-spicy. For children: use a naturally sweet sweet potato, omit gochugaru, serve the rice and sweet potato plain or with a tiny amount of soy-sesame sauce, and cut the sweet potato into small, soft pieces. Because the sweet potato cooks directly with the rice, it becomes soft and naturally sweet.

groups.title: For the rice (about 2–3 servings)
items: 1 medium Korean/Japanese sweet potato, about 250–300 g
1½ cups water, approximately, adjusted for the rice and soaking

groups.title: Seasoning sauce
items: 1 Tbsp finely chopped Asian chives or scallions
Optional: ½ tsp gochugaru for adults

method: Rinse the rice several times until the water becomes relatively clear.
Put the rice in a pot and add water. Let it soak for about 30 minutes.
Peel the sweet potato and rinse it.
Cut it into roughly ½-inch / 1.25-cm cubes.
Scatter the sweet-potato cubes evenly over the soaked rice.
Bring the pot to a boil over medium heat.
Cook for about 10 minutes in a regular pot.
Open the lid and gently turn the rice and sweet potato together.
Cover again and reduce the heat.
Simmer another 10–15 minutes, until the rice and sweet potato are fully cooked.
Mix the soy sauce, chives/scallions, garlic, honey, vinegar and sesame seeds to make the seasoning sauce.
Serve the sweet-potato rice with the sauce on the side, allowing each person to season their own bowl.
recipes.story: The clever part is that the sweet potato isn't treated as a separate side dish. It cooks right on top of the rice, so its sweetness and moisture become part of the finished bowl. It's also a nice example for Rasalaya of a seasonal ingredient crossing into an everyday staple: the same harvest crop can be eaten simply rather than transformed into a complicated autumn recipe.

sources.name: Maangchi — Korean recipes made with sweet potato

recipes.name: Chinese Lotus Root Soup
recipes.region: China — particularly southern Chinese home cooking
recipes.seasonWhy: Lotus root is strongly associated with autumn harvest cooking in China, and its crisp texture and availability make it particularly suited to seasonal soups. Lotus root brings a distinctly Asian autumn ingredient and visual identity to the collection — autumn doesn't have to mean only orange squash and warming spices.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES; VEGAN: YES for the version specified here. This is important because some Chinese lotus-root soups traditionally use pork ribs, chicken or other meat. The Rasalaya version should explicitly use mushrooms and peanuts for body and flavor rather than meat. Food Network Kitchen identifies its lotus-root soup as vegan.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: With a simple adaptation: slice the lotus root thinly so it is easier to chew, use fewer ginger slices, keep the broth lightly salted, serve soft carrots, peanuts only if age-appropriate, and tender lotus root; for younger children, strain the broth and serve the soft vegetables separately. Because the soup is mild and slightly sweet from the carrots and dates, it does not need chili or strong seasoning.

method: Soak the dried shiitake mushrooms in warm water until softened, usually 20–30 minutes. Reserve the soaking liquid if it is clean.
Soak the peanuts for several hours or overnight if desired.
Peel the lotus root and slice it into rounds.
Peel the carrots and cut them into thick pieces.
Slice the ginger.
Put the lotus root, carrots, mushrooms, peanuts, red dates and ginger into a large soup pot.
Add about 8 cups water.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer.
Cover partially and cook until the lotus root, peanuts and carrots are tender — about 1½–2 hours for a deeply flavored soup.
Season with salt toward the end.
Taste and adjust the seasoning.
Serve hot, with the lotus-root slices and other ingredients in the bowl along with the broth.
recipes.story: The cross-section of lotus root has a distinctive pattern of holes, which makes it immediately recognizable in the bowl. Those holes aren't just decorative: they are part of the lotus plant's internal air-channel system. It also gives Rasalaya a nice cultural counterpoint to the first five dishes: autumn seasonal cooking can be based on harvest availability and traditional food culture without relying on Western “fall” flavor conventions.

sources.name: Food Network Kitchen — Chinese Lotus Root Soup

recipes.name: Castagnaccio
recipes.seasonWhy: Chestnuts are traditionally harvested in autumn in Tuscany and other Italian mountain regions; chestnut flour was historically made from the autumn harvest and stored through the year. The rosemary, nuts and dried-fruit flavours fit the cooler-season pantry. Best months: October–November.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES — also vegan, dairy-free, egg-free and naturally gluten-free. Traditional castagnaccio contains no butter, eggs or milk.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: An easy adaptation exists for children: reduce the rosemary slightly, chop the walnuts finely, use extra raisins for natural sweetness, and serve in small squares like snack bars. Note the texture is unusual for children expecting cake — it is more like a dense chestnut brownie or polenta slice.

groups.title: Add-ins
items: Fresh rosemary needles, from 1–2 small sprigs

groups.title: Finishing
items: 1–2 Tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, for drizzling

method: Place the raisins in warm water and soak for 10 minutes until softened.
Preheat the oven to 180°C / 350°F.
Sift the chestnut flour into a large mixing bowl.
Add the salt.
Slowly pour in the water while whisking continuously to prevent lumps.
Add the olive oil and mix until the batter is smooth.
Drain the raisins and squeeze out excess water.
Stir half the raisins, half the pine nuts and half the walnuts into the batter.
Oil a shallow baking pan generously.
Pour the batter into the pan — it should be relatively thin, about 1–2 cm deep.
Scatter the remaining nuts and raisins over the top.
Sprinkle the rosemary needles over the surface.
Drizzle with olive oil.
Bake for approximately 30–35 minutes, until the surface develops characteristic cracks.
Cool before slicing.
recipes.story: Castagnaccio is a beautiful example of “poor cuisine” becoming heritage cuisine. For centuries, chestnuts were called the “bread tree” in some mountain regions, because chestnut flour could provide calories when wheat was scarce — the original dish was a practical way to turn stored chestnut flour into nourishing food, not a luxury dessert. A traditional Tuscan belief also associated rosemary with romance and courtship, giving the herb a folkloric role beyond flavour.

sources.name: Recipes from Italy — Traditional Tuscan Castagnaccio

recipes.name: Krupnik
recipes.seasonWhy: Uses barley, a traditional cool-weather grain, and dried mushrooms historically gathered in autumn and preserved for winter soups; root vegetables make it a hearty cold-weather soup. Peak season: October–February.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN VERSION: YES — uses vegetable stock instead of meat stock, mushrooms for depth, and no meat products. Traditional versions may contain meat or meat broth, so Rasalaya labels this specifically “Vegetarian Krupnik (mushroom-barley version)”.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: An easy adaptation exists for children: chop the vegetables very finely, use mild mushrooms such as cremini, reduce the pepper, and add a little sour cream or yogurt swirl if dairy is used. The barley texture makes it similar to familiar rice soups.

method: Soak the dried mushrooms in hot water for 20–30 minutes.
Remove the mushrooms and chop finely.
Strain the soaking liquid to remove grit.
Heat the olive oil or butter in a soup pot.
Add the onion and cook until soft.
Add the carrots and celery; cook for 5 minutes.
Add the fresh mushrooms and dried mushrooms.
Cook until the mushrooms release their aroma.
Add the barley and stir briefly.
Add the vegetable stock and the mushroom soaking liquid.
Add the bay leaf and pepper.
Simmer for 30–40 minutes, until the barley becomes tender.
Add the potatoes halfway through cooking so they remain intact.
Adjust the seasoning.
Finish with dill or parsley.
Serve warm with optional sour cream.
recipes.story: Krupnik shows how Eastern European cuisines preserved forest foods. Wild mushrooms were traditionally gathered in autumn, dried, and saved for soups during winter when fresh produce was limited — the dried mushrooms provide the deep savoury flavour that makes the vegetarian version satisfying without meat broth.

sources.name: The Nosher — Vegetarian Mushroom Barley Soup
Everyday Healthy Recipes — Polish Krupnik Barley Soup

recipes.name: Pumpkin Gnocchi
recipes.seasonWhy: Pumpkin is an iconic autumn harvest ingredient; the dish traditionally uses winter squash harvested in late summer and autumn. Warm sage, butter and cheese pair naturally with cooler weather.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES — with an important note: use vegetarian-certified Parmesan or vegetarian hard cheese, because many traditional Parmesan cheeses use animal-derived rennet. The recipe below assumes vegetarian-certified Parmesan.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: An easy adaptation exists for children: use sweeter pumpkin varieties, reduce the nutmeg, serve with a simple butter or olive-oil sauce, and cut the gnocchi smaller. Children often enjoy the soft dumpling texture and mild sweetness.

groups.title: Gnocchi dough (serves 4)
items: 500 g pumpkin or butternut squash purée

method: Roast the pumpkin pieces until tender and the moisture has evaporated.
Mash or purée the pumpkin.
Combine the pumpkin with the mashed potato.
Add the egg, salt and nutmeg.
Add the flour gradually until a soft dough forms.
Avoid adding too much flour — the gnocchi should remain tender.
Divide the dough into portions.
Roll each portion into ropes about 2 cm thick.
Cut into small pillow-shaped pieces.
Optional: press lightly with a fork to create ridges.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a gentle boil.
Cook the gnocchi in batches.
When they float to the surface, remove with a slotted spoon.
Melt the butter in a pan.
Add the sage leaves and warm until fragrant.
Toss the cooked gnocchi in the sage butter.
Finish with vegetarian-certified Parmesan and black pepper.
Serve immediately.
recipes.story: Pumpkin gnocchi reflects northern Italy’s tradition of transforming inexpensive seasonal crops into comforting dishes. Mantua’s cuisine is especially famous for pumpkin preparations — including pumpkin-filled pasta and pumpkin gnocchi — where the sweetness of pumpkin is traditionally balanced with savoury cheese, nutmeg and herbs.

sources.name: Food.com — Northern Italian Pumpkin Gnocchi with Sage Butter

recipes.name: Sabudana Khichdi
recipes.seasonWhy: Festival: Sharad Navratri / vrat — especially appropriate October 11–19, 2026. Sabudana khichdi is one of the most recognizable vrat foods associated with Navratri, as well as Ekadashi and Maha Shivratri. Its importance comes from the fasting-food system in which sabudana is treated as an acceptable non-grain ingredient.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES. The standard vrat formulation uses sabudana, potato, peanuts, cumin, lemon and vegetable oil or ghee, with no meat, fish or eggs. It is also gluten-free and grain-free in the culinary sense relevant to vrat cooking. Vegan: potentially yes if prepared with oil rather than ghee.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Naturally kid-adaptable, but no distinct historical “children's version” is necessary. For children: omit green chili, reduce sendha namak, use finely diced, very soft potatoes, keep the peanut pieces coarse enough to retain texture but appropriately prepared for the child's age, and serve with plain yogurt. The naturally mild, slightly chewy pearls and soft potato make the basic dish approachable to children.

groups.title: Serves 3–4
items: 1 cup / approximately 150–200 g medium sabudana (tapioca pearls)
About ¾ cup / 180 ml water, for soaking
½ cup / 75 g raw peanuts, roasted and coarsely crushed
2 medium potatoes, peeled and diced small
1 tsp sendha namak (rock salt), or to taste

method: Rinse the sabudana several times until the water is mostly clear.
Put it in a bowl and add enough water to just wet/cover the pearls rather than leaving them submerged in a large volume.
Soak for about 4–8 hours or overnight, depending on the sabudana. A pearl should crush easily between your fingers when properly hydrated.
Drain very thoroughly and allow the sabudana to rest for about 20–30 minutes.
Dry-roast the peanuts until fragrant. Cool and crush them coarsely.
Mix the drained sabudana with the crushed peanuts, sugar and sendha namak.
Heat oil or ghee in a wide pan.
Add cumin seeds and let them sizzle.
Add diced potato and cook until tender and lightly golden.
Add green chili if using.
Add the sabudana-peanut mixture.
Toss gently over medium-low heat. Don't mash or aggressively stir the pearls.
Cook until the sabudana becomes translucent and glossy, generally about 5–8 minutes.
Turn off the heat.
Add lemon juice and coriander.
Serve hot, traditionally with plain or sweetened yogurt.
recipes.story: The deceptively simple dish has a reputation for being technically tricky: the soak determines the texture. Too much water and the pearls become sticky; correctly hydrated pearls remain separate, translucent and pleasantly chewy. It is also interesting that sabudana isn't a grain at all: the pearls are made from tapioca/cassava starch. That helps explain its place in many fasting-food traditions.

sources.name: Raks Kitchen — Sabudana Khichdi, Vrat Recipe
Easy Indian Cookbook — Maharashtrian Sabudana Khichdi

recipes.name: Sabudana Vada
recipes.seasonWhy: Festival: Sharad Navratri / vrat. Sabudana vada is explicitly documented as a fasting food, including during Navratri. It is also associated with other Hindu fasting occasions such as Ekadashi and Maha Shivratri. Sharad Navratri: October 11–19, 2026; Dussehra/Vijayadashami: October 20, 2026.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES. The documented fasting recipe contains sabudana, potato, peanuts, herbs, spices, lemon and frying oil and is explicitly described as vegan. Vegan: yes, when fried in vegetable/peanut oil rather than ghee.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Adaptation rather than a separate traditional children's recipe. For children: omit green chili, omit ginger if desired, use finely mashed potato, make smaller, thinner patties, and serve with plain yogurt instead of spicy chutney. The interior becomes soft and potato-rich while the outside remains crisp.

groups.title: Makes approximately 12–14 vadas
items: 3 medium potatoes / about 350 g, boiled, peeled and mashed
½ cup / 75 g roasted peanuts, skinned and coarsely ground
1 tsp grated fresh ginger — optional depending on fasting practice
1 tsp sendha namak, or to taste
Peanut oil or another suitable frying oil, for deep-frying

method: Rinse the sabudana.
Soak it for approximately 4–5 hours, using only enough water to hydrate it.
Drain it extremely well and leave it in a colander for at least 20 minutes.
Boil the potatoes until completely tender.
Peel and mash them while warm.
Roast the peanuts and grind them coarsely.
Combine sabudana, mashed potato and peanuts.
Add cumin, sendha namak, sugar, lemon juice, coriander and optional ginger and green chili.
Mix gently until the mixture holds together when pressed.
Grease your hands.
Take a small portion and flatten it into a patty about 1 cm thick.
Shape all the vadas before beginning to fry.
Heat the oil over medium heat.
Test with a tiny piece of mixture: it should rise steadily without immediately browning.
Fry 4–5 vadas at a time.
Leave them undisturbed initially so the exterior firms up.
Turn once and fry until crisp and deep golden.
Drain on paper towels.
Serve hot, traditionally with vrat-style chutney or yogurt.
recipes.story: Sabudana vada is a great example of how texture is engineered without wheat or another flour. Potato starch and ground peanuts bind the hydrated tapioca pearls together, so the mixture can be shaped into patties without a conventional flour binder. Its texture is deliberately contrasting: crisp outside, soft and chewy inside.

sources.name: Dassana's Veg Recipes — Sabudana Vada for Fasting

recipes.name: Kuttu Ki Puri
recipes.seasonWhy: Festival: Sharad Navratri / vrat. Kuttu is one of the principal flours used in North Indian fasting cuisine. Kuttu puri is specifically documented as a food prepared during Sharad Navratri, as well as other fasting occasions. It illustrates an important principle of vrat cuisine: buckwheat is botanically a seed rather than a conventional cereal grain, yet its flour can be turned into a bread-like food.
recipes.vegNote: VEGETARIAN: YES. The documented fasting versions contain buckwheat flour, potato, rock salt and either ghee or vegetable/peanut oil. Vegan: only if fried in vegetable/peanut oil rather than ghee. Gluten-free: buckwheat itself is gluten-free, but certified gluten-free flour is recommended for people with celiac disease because cross-contamination can occur.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Simple adaptation. For children: omit green chili, use a little less pepper, make small puris, roll them slightly thicker so they remain soft inside, and serve with plain yogurt or mild potato curry. Because kuttu can have a distinctive earthy flavor, the potato-rich dough is generally the gentler introduction for children.

groups.title: Makes approximately 10–12 puris
items: 240–250 g / about 2 cups kuttu atta (buckwheat flour)
125–250 g boiled potato, mashed very smooth (about 200 g for a flexible dough)
½ tsp freshly ground black pepper
2–3 Tbsp warm water, only if necessary
Ghee or peanut oil, for deep-frying
Additional kuttu flour or greased parchment, for shaping

method: Boil the potatoes until completely soft.
Peel and mash them until smooth, with no large lumps.
Sift the kuttu flour into a wide bowl.
Add sendha namak and optional pepper/ajwain.
Add the mashed potato.
Mix and knead gently with your fingers.
Add a little warm water only if necessary. The dough should be soft enough to shape but not wet.
Cover and rest for about 20–30 minutes.
Divide into small balls.
Because kuttu dough is fragile and gluten-free, flatten each ball carefully between lightly greased sheets or on a lightly greased surface.
Roll into small rounds, roughly 3–4 inches across.
Heat ghee or peanut oil in a deep pan.
Test the temperature with a small piece of dough; it should rise promptly.
Slide one puri carefully into the hot fat.
Gently press the center with a slotted spoon to encourage puffing.
Turn once and fry until cooked and lightly golden.
Drain.
Repeat with the remaining puris.
Serve hot with vrat-friendly potato curry, yogurt or another permitted accompaniment.
recipes.story: The most interesting technical fact is that kuttu flour has no gluten, so a normal wheat-style dough technique doesn't work. The boiled potato supplies the binding structure that lets cooks roll and fry the puris. That also explains why kuttu puris can be challenging for beginners: the dough is much more fragile than ordinary atta dough.

sources.name: Panchangya — Kuttu Ki Puri, Vrat Recipe
Dassana's Veg Recipes — Kuttu Ki Puri / Vrat Ki Poori

recipes.name: Samak Rice Khichdi
recipes.region: North and western India (Maharashtra and Gujarat)
recipes.seasonWhy: Sharad Navratri / Navratri vrat — October 11–19, 2026; associated with the wider Dussehra period culminating October 20. Samak is one of the traditional foods used in Hindu fasting when ordinary cereal grains and pulses are avoided. Database note: the festival connection is stronger than a seasonal/harvest connection here — its place in the collection comes from religious fasting tradition, not from October being the natural harvest season for samak.
recipes.vegNote: YES — vegetarian. It can also be vegan if ghee is replaced with vegetable or peanut oil.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: For children: omit green chili and ginger if desired, use soft, small potato cubes, reduce black pepper, make the khichdi softer with a little additional water, and serve with plain yogurt if dairy is permitted. This is naturally a fairly approachable children's dish because it is soft and spoonable.

groups.title: Makes about 3 servings
items: 1 cup / 180 g samak (barnyard millet), rinsed and soaked for 20 minutes
1 medium potato, about 120 g, peeled and diced
1 tsp sendha namak, or to taste

groups.title: Optional
items: 1 small tomato, diced, if permitted by the household's fasting tradition

method: Rinse the samak thoroughly and soak for about 20 minutes. Drain.
Heat the ghee in a heavy pan or pressure cooker.
Add the peanuts and sauté for about 2 minutes until lightly toasted.
Add cumin seeds; once fragrant, add ginger and optional green chili.
Add the diced potato and sauté for about 3 minutes.
Add the drained samak, sendha namak and black pepper. Stir gently for about a minute.
Add the hot water.
Pressure-cooker method: cook for 1 whistle over medium heat, then allow the pressure to release naturally.
Stovetop method: cover and simmer for roughly 12–15 minutes, until the millet is tender and the mixture is soft and spoonable.
Stir gently and adjust the consistency with a little hot water if needed.
Finish with lemon juice and coriander. Serve hot, traditionally with vrat-friendly yogurt/curd.
recipes.story: The name “samak rice” is misleading: samak is barnyard millet, not rice. The “rice” terminology comes from its use as a rice substitute during fasting. Different regions give the same little grain different names — sama, samak, samvat, bhagar, moraiyo, sanwa and others.

sources.name: Dassana's Veg Recipes — Samak Rice Pulao / Barnyard Millet

recipes.name: Singhara Atta Cheela
recipes.seasonWhy: Sharad Navratri / Navratri vrat — October 11–19, 2026. Singhara atta is a classic fasting flour used when wheat and other ordinary grains are avoided. The seasonal classification here is festival-based rather than agricultural-season-based: it belongs in the autumn collection because Sharad Navratri falls in October 2026.
recipes.vegNote: YES — vegetarian. It can be vegan when cooked with oil rather than ghee and served without dairy. It is also naturally gluten-free, although anyone with celiac disease should use appropriately certified flour to avoid cross-contact.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: A child-friendly version can: omit green chili, use very little black pepper, make smaller, thicker pancakes, serve with mild plain yogurt, and optionally add finely grated potato for a softer texture. This is particularly easy to adapt because the basic batter contains no inherently spicy ingredients.

groups.title: Makes about 4 medium cheelas
items: ¾ cup / about 90 g singhara atta (water chestnut flour)
½ tsp black pepper, freshly ground
½–1 green chili, finely chopped — optional
½ tsp sendha namak, or to taste
About ¾–1 cup water, as needed
2–3 tsp ghee or neutral oil for cooking

groups.title: Optional additions
items: a little grated potato or other vrat-permitted vegetable, depending on household practice

method: Put the singhara atta into a mixing bowl.
Add cumin, black pepper, coriander, optional green chili and sendha namak.
Gradually add water while whisking to form a smooth, pourable batter.
Let the batter rest for about 10 minutes; add a little more water if it thickens.
Heat a lightly greased tawa or nonstick pan over medium heat.
Pour a ladleful of batter onto the pan.
Gently spread it into a round shape. Don't make it excessively thin because singhara batter is more fragile than wheat-based batter.
Drizzle a little ghee/oil around the edges.
Cook for roughly 2–3 minutes until the underside is set and lightly browned.
Carefully flip and cook the second side for another 1–2 minutes.
Serve hot with plain yogurt or a fasting-compatible chutney.
recipes.story: The interesting ingredient here is water chestnut flour rather than a conventional grain flour. During Navratri, singhara atta provides a way to make something resembling a pancake/flatbread while observing fasting food restrictions.

sources.name: Hindustan Times — Singhara Atta Cheela for Navratri fasting

recipes.name: Dahi Aloo
recipes.region: Rajasthan and western Uttar Pradesh (documented vrat preparation)
recipes.seasonWhy: Sharad Navratri / Navratri vrat — October 11–19, 2026. Dahi Aloo fits the festival collection because its vrat form is specifically used on Navratri fasting days and uses ingredients accepted within common phalahar/vrat traditions: potatoes, yogurt, sendha namak and fasting flours rather than ordinary besan or grain-based ingredients. It is also used during other fasting observances such as Ekadashi and Chaitra Navratri, so it should not be labeled as exclusively a Sharad Navratri dish.
recipes.vegNote: YES — vegetarian. It can be made vegan with unsweetened plant yogurt and oil instead of ghee, although that becomes a modern adaptation rather than the traditional dairy-based version.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: For children: omit green chili, reduce black pepper, use mild, fresh yogurt, keep potato pieces soft and relatively large, retain the small amount of sugar, which balances the yogurt's tang, and serve with a mild vrat flatbread or plain rice substitute.

groups.title: Serves about 4
items: 1 Tbsp singhara atta or kuttu atta
1 tsp sendha namak, or to taste

method: Boil the potatoes until tender but not falling apart.
Peel them and break them into rough chunks rather than finely chopping them.
Whisk the yogurt until smooth.
Whisk the singhara or kuttu flour into the yogurt with about ½ cup of the water until completely lump-free.
Heat the ghee in a kadhai over medium heat.
Add cumin seeds.
Add ginger and optional green chili; sauté briefly.
Add the potatoes and cook for 3–4 minutes, lightly pressing a few pieces so some potato thickens the gravy.
Lower the heat.
Slowly pour in the yogurt mixture while stirring continuously in one direction. This helps prevent the yogurt from splitting.
Once it reaches a gentle boil, add the remaining water, sendha namak, black pepper and sugar.
Simmer uncovered for about 8–10 minutes, until the gravy thickens enough to coat a spoon.
Garnish with coriander and serve hot, traditionally alongside kuttu puri, rajgira paratha or samak rice.
recipes.story: The interesting culinary trick is that fasting rules change the thickener. On an ordinary preparation, gram flour (besan) may be used, but in this vrat version, singhara or kuttu flour takes over that job. The flour also helps stabilize the yogurt so the gravy doesn't split as easily.

sources.name: Hetal Kamdar — Vrat Ke Dahi Aloo

recipes.name: Makhana Kheer
recipes.region: North India / broader North and Central Indian festive cuisine
recipes.seasonWhy: Sharad Navratri / Navratri vrat — October 11–19, 2026. Makhana kheer is explicitly documented as a food for Sharad Navratri fasting, as well as other Hindu fasting observances such as Ekadashi, Janmashtami and Mahashivaratri. For the 2026 collection, its October placement is festival-based rather than harvest-season-based.
recipes.vegNote: YES — vegetarian. It is traditionally made with milk and ghee. A vegan adaptation can use plant milk and vegan fat, although that is a modern adaptation rather than the classic preparation.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Naturally kid-friendly. Possible adaptation: reduce or omit saffron if children don't like it, use finely crushed makhana for a smoother texture, reduce the nuts or grind them finely for younger children, serve chilled if preferred, and keep the sweetness moderate. For very young children, nuts should of course be prepared in an age-appropriate form.

groups.title: Makes about 4 servings
items: ⅓ cup / about 70 g sugar, or to taste
1 Tbsp warm milk for soaking saffron, if using

method: Heat the ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan over low heat.
Add the makhana and roast for about 5–6 minutes, stirring frequently, until crisp.
Test one: it should crush easily between your fingers.
Remove from the pan and allow to cool slightly.
Coarsely crush about half of the makhana, leaving the rest whole or in large pieces. This gives the finished kheer contrasting textures.
In the same pan, lightly sauté the almonds and cashews for about a minute.
In a separate heavy-bottomed saucepan, bring the milk to a boil.
Reduce the heat and add the roasted makhana.
Simmer gently for about 15–20 minutes, stirring periodically so the milk doesn't scorch.
Add the sugar and cardamom.
Add the raisins, pistachios and optional saffron.
Continue simmering until the milk thickens and the makhana becomes soft.
Serve warm or chilled. Remember that kheer thickens further as it cools.
recipes.story: Makhana behaves surprisingly like a grain in kheer: when roasted, crushed and simmered in milk, it releases enough starchiness to help the pudding become creamy. That's why it can stand in for rice in a kheer even though it isn't rice. A particularly nice Rasalaya fact is that one ingredient can appear in both savory and sweet vrat dishes: roasted makhana is eaten as a snack, while the same ingredient becomes a creamy festival dessert.

sources.name: Dassana's Veg Recipes — Makhane Ki Kheer

recipes.name: Jalebi
recipes.seasonWhy: Dussehra / Vijayadashami — October 20, 2026. Jalebi has a particularly strong Dussehra/festival association in contemporary Indian food culture. Important classification: this is a Dussehra festive sweet, not a standard Navratri vrat food. Traditional jalebi contains maida, so it should not be placed in the same fasting-food category as sabudana, kuttu, singhara or samak.
recipes.vegNote: YES — vegetarian. The traditional recipe contains flour, gram flour, sugar and oil/ghee and contains no meat or fish. The cited recipe also identifies its jalebi as vegetarian/vegan when made with plant oil rather than ghee.

kidVersion.title: Kids love it
kidVersion.text: Jalebi is naturally appealing to children, although it is a high-sugar fried sweet. For a kid-friendly serving: make smaller spirals, make them slightly less thick and easier to bite, allow excess syrup to drain, and serve as a small festive portion rather than an everyday snack. There is no separate historical “children's jalebi” version.

groups.title: Batter (makes approximately 18–20 jalebis)
items: ⅛ tsp turmeric powder, for natural color
Additional 1–2 Tbsp maida after fermentation, if necessary

groups.title: For frying
items: Neutral high-heat oil or ghee, as required

method: Combine maida, besan, turmeric and baking soda.
Gradually add water to make a smooth, flowing but moderately thick batter.
Whisk/stir vigorously for several minutes to aerate it.
Cover and leave somewhere warm to ferment.
Depending on temperature, fermentation may take roughly 6–24 hours; a moderate room temperature commonly takes around 12–15 hours.
Once fermented, stir the batter. Add a little additional maida if it has become too thin.
Transfer the batter to a squeeze bottle, piping bag or similar container with a small opening.
For the syrup, combine sugar and water in a saucepan.
Add saffron and cook until the syrup reaches approximately one-string consistency.
Stir in the lemon juice and keep the syrup warm.
Heat the frying oil/ghee to approximately 350°F / 176°C.
Carefully squeeze the batter into the hot fat in concentric spirals.
Fry until crisp and lightly golden, turning as necessary.
Remove and drain briefly.
Immediately transfer the jalebi into the warm sugar syrup.
Turn once so both sides are coated and soak for roughly 2–3 minutes.
Remove and drain excess syrup.
Serve warm, at room temperature, or with milk/rabri.
recipes.story: One of jalebi's defining characteristics is the contrast between crisp fried batter and liquid sugar syrup. The batter is fried into spirals and then soaked while the syrup is still warm. The fermentation also gives traditional jalebi its characteristic slight tang, which balances the sweetness. Jalebi vs. Imarti: both are spiral-shaped, syrup-soaked Indian sweets, but jalebi is flour-based, while imarti/jangiri is made from urad-dal batter. So they should be linked but not treated as aliases.

sources.name: NDTV Food — Celebrate Dussehra With Jalebi
